items.abstract: <jats:p>Extreme-ultraviolet lithography (EUVL) mask absorber patterns inherently form trapezoidal cross-sectional profiles, characterized by a sidewall angle (SWA), because of process limitations. However, this feature has often been considered a fabrication imperfection rather than an optical design parameter. To assess process tolerance, we systematically investigate how the geometric profile and optical constants of mask absorbers influence imaging performance in next-generation high-numerical aperture (NA) EUVL. A tapered sidewall alters the scattering condition at the absorber edge and thereby redistributes the amplitude and phase of the diffracted orders. These changes affect the key imaging metrics, including the normalized image log slope, best focus shift, and horizontal–vertical bias. The sensitivity to SWA variation depends strongly on the absorber material’s optical constants. In particular, a high extinction coefficient and a refractive index approaching unity substantially reduce the impact of SWA variation, thereby improving process tolerance. These findings show that absorber geometry and material properties jointly govern imaging behavior in high-NA EUV systems and provide guidelines for designing next-generation absorber materials with reduced sensitivity to SWA variation.</jats:p>
title: Impact of mask absorber geometry on imaging stability in extreme-ultraviolet lithography with high numerical aperture

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundThe semiconductor industry strives to enhance lithography resolution in response to the demand for miniaturization and improved performance in electronic devices. The introduction of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, utilizing a short wavelength of 13.5 nm, has facilitated high-resolution patterning. However, the transition to EUV is constrained by limited photon availability at a given source power, resulting in photon shot noise that complicates the reduction of line edge roughness (LER) and defect removal.AimWe explore the potential for overcoming these challenges by combining directed self-assembly (DSA) of block copolymers (BCP) with EUV lithography and investigate methods for achieving high-quality patterning by modifying polymer chain architectures.ApproachWe performed Monte Carlo (MC) simulations with a coarse-grained model to compare the DSA behavior of linear block copolymers (LBCP) and Janus-type bottlebrush polymers (JBBP) on EUV-patterned guide templates with various roughness conditions.ResultsOur results demonstrate that DSA of linear block copolymers reduces LER and eliminates bridge defects. Furthermore, Janus-type bottlebrush polymers, with densely grafted homopolymer side chains of different types, reduce pattern roughness compared with LBCP.ConclusionsThese findings demonstrate that JBBP architecture offers superior roughness reduction, whereas LBCP provides robust defect tolerance, establishing design guidelines for advanced EUV+ DSA patterning technologies.</jats:p>
title: Directed self-assembly of linear and Janus-type bottlebrush block copolymers for enhanced EUV lithography pattern quality

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundPattern placement accuracy in high-numerical-aperture (NA) extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography is constrained by mask-induced image split in the aerial image, resulting from mask 3D effects under off-axis illumination (OAI). This image split stems from pole-dependent phase asymmetry between diffraction orders generated by the thick, reflective EUV mask stack, with increased severity for fine-pitch patterning in high-NA systems. The conventional approach of targeting zero phase delta (Δϕ) between the zeroth and first diffraction orders is suboptimal (could not suppress image split under realistic OAI conditions). Source averaging over finite illumination angles disrupts the symmetry assumed in simplified interference models, rendering Δϕ=0 ineffective for image alignment.AimThis study proposes and validates a design paradigm, termed active phase engineering, which treats Δϕ as an actively optimized parameter. Rigorous coupled-wave analysis for 0.33 and 0.55 NA systems demonstrates that the phase delta minimizing image split is generally nonzero and depends on pattern pitch.ApproachBy analyzing a broad absorber parameter space, we derive a quantitative design curve that directly relates the optimal Δϕ to the target half-pitch. For a representative 12 nm half-pitch, tuning the mask phase to this predicted target value suppresses image split, reduces the normalized image log-slope penalty, and yields a sharper aerial image.ResultsActively controlling mask-induced phase—rather than enforcing a zero-phase condition—preserves image fidelity and pattern placement accuracy in high-NA EUV lithography.ConclusionThe active phase engineering framework therefore provides a practical and quantitative guideline for next-generation EUV mask design across 0.33 to 0.55 NA systems.</jats:p>
title: Active phase engineering of extreme ultraviolet masks for mitigating pitch-dependent image split

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundThree-dimensional mask (M3D) effects in EUV lithography arise from complex electromagnetic scattering associated with the three-dimensional geometry of mask absorbers and multilayer stacks. Historically, M3D effects have been regarded as detrimental to process performance.AimThis study aims to offer an alternative perspective on M3D effects in EUV lithography. We demonstrate that M3D effects can be harnessed under certain conditions to improve imaging fidelity for high-NA and hyper-NA EUV lithography.ApproachWe performed fully rigorous source-mask optimizations (SMO) for different line-space (L/S) configurations to compare the achievable performance of M3D with Kirchhoff-type flat masks and to identify the best imaging solutions for both.ResultsM3D with L/S on dark-field masks can outperform Kirchhoff-type masks in terms of efficient use of EUV light, achievable contrast, and depth of focus (DoF). Realizing these benefits requires split-pupil exposure or other techniques to offset the contrast loss due to M3D-induced image fading. In-depth analyses of near-fields, diffraction, and aerial images explain the advantages of 3D dark-field masks: more efficient light coupling into diffraction orders within the projection NA and tighter, higher near-field intensity peaks due to light guiding in low-n absorbers. The benefits of M3D are less pronounced for bright-field masks and for horizontal L/S near the resolution limit of hyper-NA systems.ConclusionsM3D effects, when combined with rigorous SMO and split-pupil exposure, can enhance imaging in high-NA EUV lithography and hyper-NA regimes. These benefits are use-case-dependent and have a significant impact on OPC and SMO strategies in terms of biasing, assist sizes, and optimum source shapes.</jats:p>
title: Benefits of three-dimensional mask (M3D) effects in high-NA and hyper-NA EUV lithography

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundIn the single-wafer wet cleaning process, a large amount of IPA mixed wastewater is discharged as organic wastewater. As semiconductor layer structures become more complex, organic wastewater is expected to increase further. The treatment of organic wastewater emits large amounts of CO2, placing a burden on the environment.AimWe are aiming to develop a system that separates IPA from IPA mixed wastewater and reuses it in the original cleaning process.ApproachWe examined the approach of separating IPA and water using a zeolite membrane. We prepared the IPA/water separation tool on a small scale and constructed a simulation model to match the experimental tool.ResultsUsing this experimental tool, we were able to concentrate IPA mixed water with an IPA concentration of 20 wt% to 99.6 wt%. Furthermore, simulation results could match the experimental results within a 3 wt% variation range.ConclusionsBy utilizing separation technology with zeolite membranes, water was removed from the IPA mixture and concentrated to a reclaimable level of IPA concentration. The simulation results also suggested the possibility of scaling up the results of this experiment.</jats:p>
title: Reduction of organic wastewater by isopropyl alcohol/water separation technology using zeolite membrane

items.abstract: <jats:p>Constructing a dense focus–exposure matrix (FEM) for lithographic process-window analysis is often limited by the cost of acquiring (real or synthetic) scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images at every focus and dose condition. We propose a layout-to-SEM generative surrogate, PADE (process-adaptive denormalization), that injects the lithographic process condition (exposure dose, focus level, or both) into every denormalization layer of an image-to-image translation backbone, paired with a variational latent that supplies the cell-specific SEM texture. It can synthesize SEM images corresponding to unseen intermediate conditions in a single forward pass by interpolating the per-cell encoded latent and feeding the target condition directly to the generator after training on a sparse grid of focus–dose anchors only. On a 3×3 focus–dose anchor grid over 40 line–space cells rendered by a physics-based simulation pipeline, the generated SEM images successfully reconstruct the simulated FEM with accurate metrology metrics. For example, the critical dimension measured from the generated SEM images precisely tracks the simulated ground-truth values with a Pearson correlation of r=0.999 and a root-mean-square error of 1.72 nm. The exposure latitude extracted from the generated Bossung surfaces also agrees well with the ground truth at r=0.97. Once trained, PADE can produce SEM images almost in real time (7108 times faster than conventional physics-based simulation), enabling continuous Bossung-curve extraction and comprehensive process-window analysis in process development.</jats:p>
title: PADE: process-adaptive denormalization for focus–dose conditioned SEM image generation

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundSuboptimal layout geometries following optical proximity correction (OPC) may lead to lithography hotspots, adversely impacting wafer yield. Conventional hotspot correction techniques, including rule-based and model-based methods, frequently fall short due to their time-intensive nature and limitations in model accuracy.AimWe present a lithography hotspot correction methodology employing generative adversarial networks (GANs) to refine hotspot geometries and improve lithographic fidelity of design layouts. In addition, the proposed approach seeks to enhance correction efficiency relative to traditional methods.ApproachA hotspot correction model is developed based on various lithography rule check (LRC) hotspot types. A pix2pix GAN model is trained using paired post-OPC layout images and simulated after-development inspection contour images generated via an LRC tool. Hotspot-free contours serve as input to generate predicted hotspot-free mask layouts, subsequently converted to polygonal formats and integrated into original masks for LRC validation. Transfer learning is further employed to generalize the model to additional hotspot patterns. The approach is evaluated using both simulation and wafer datasets, demonstrating improvements in critical dimension (CD) accuracy and reductions in training duration.ResultsExperimental outcomes confirm that the proposed methodology efficiently corrects lithography hotspots, reducing wafer CD error below 1 nm, with maximum error reduction reaching 97.92%. In addition, the depth of focus at 4% exposure latitude improves by 27.66% while model training time is reduced to 8% of that required by conventional approaches.ConclusionsThe presented method achieves accurate, efficient hotspot correction through localized mask feature modification without introducing additional hotspots, thereby enhancing wafer yield and manufacturing throughput.</jats:p>
title: Lithography hotspot correction on post-OPC layout using generative adversarial networks

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundLateral gate-all-around (LGAA) device architectures—including nanosheet and forksheet structures—are becoming the dominant transistor platforms for sub-3 nm technology nodes. These architectures introduce multiple buried features such as silicon-germanium (SiGe) layers, dielectric-wall voids, and channel-release interfaces, many of which lie beneath hard-mask or dummy-gate stacks in actual process flows. As a result, the need for subsurface metrology that can access these features prior to or without cross-sectioning has grown substantially.AimThe aim is to isolate and evaluate the intrinsic subsurface-visibility capability of high-voltage critical-dimension scanning electron microscopy (HV CD-SEM). This study investigates its feasibility using nanosheet test structures intentionally prepared without upper hard-mask or dummy-gate layers.ApproachThree LGAA-relevant inspection targets were examined: (1) voids within dielectric walls, (2) SiGe lateral recess amounts, and (3) multilayer SiGe residues after channel release. HV CD-SEM images were acquired at elevated landing energies to enhance backscattered-electron (BSE) sensitivity to embedded features. Monte Carlo simulations were performed to interpret voltage-dependent BSE signatures, and selected features were verified by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX).ResultsHV CD-SEM successfully visualized dielectric-wall voids, extracted SiGe recess amounts using SE/BSE paired contrast, and detected SiGe residues originating from distinct depths within the nanosheet stack. Recess extraction was applied at 163 sampling locations, enabling wafer-level evaluation of layout-dependent micro-loading effects, whereas TEM cross-sections provided limited but essential reference values. Simulations correctly predicted the voltage-dependent detectability of multilayer SiGe residues, and EDX confirmed Ge-related contrast in the HV CD-SEM images.ConclusionsThese results show that HV CD-SEM possesses intrinsic subsurface-visibility capability when upper hard-mask and dummy-gate layers are absent, demonstrating feasibility for detecting voids, SiGe recess profiles, and multilayer SiGe residues in nanosheet structures. Extending this approach to fully processed LGAA devices—where upper gate-stack layers remain in place—represents an essentially next step toward establishing HV CD-SEM as a comprehensive inline subsurface metrology technique.</jats:p>
title: In-line metrology and inspection for hidden structure of lateral gate-all-around devices enabled by high voltage critical dimension scanning electron microscopy

<jats:p>BackgroundTwo-photon polymerization (TPP) enables additive manufacturing with sub-micron resolution, but fabrication accuracy is strongly limited by nonlinear exposure dynamics, radical transport, and chemical proximity effects, especially in parallelized writing setups. Simplified threshold models neglect the resist response, whereas compact models often omit key physical and time-dependent processes. Moreover, such models are typically non-differentiable, which prevents their use in solving inverse design problems.AimWe address these challenges by developing and validating a time-dependent, differentiable forward model of the TPP process and by demonstrating how it enables optimization approaches for inverse problems across different exposure conditions.ApproachWe implement the forward model in PyTorch, combining a precomputed point spread function, radical generation, oxygen quenching, diffusion, polymerization kinetics, and resist development. Based on this model, we establish two optimization strategies: (i) a gradient-based point-by-point backpropagation method to optimize power along scan paths and (ii) a hybrid approach where a neural network predicts an initial exposure strategy that is refined by the physics-based model. These methods are applied to three experimental configurations: point-by-point writing, diffractive optical element (DOE)-based parallel exposure, and spatial light modulator (SLM) projection.ResultsWe demonstrate that the forward model, combined with inverse optimization, derives exposure distributions directly from target structures and improves fabrication accuracy in all three cases. In point-by-point writing, backpropagation adjusts power to control feature height and connectivity in three-dimensional structures. In DOE-based parallelization, the framework predicts line merging and height loss at the start and end of lines caused by oxygen inhibition and compensates for them through local dose control. In SLM projection with a low-contrast resist, the U-Net-assisted workflow produces optimized exposure distributions that enable the fabrication of microlens arrays and freeform features consistent with the design targets within the material’s resolution limits.ConclusionsThe presented time-dependent, differentiable forward model enables gradient-based optimization of exposure conditions across different TPP setups. This provides a scalable tool for dose correction and lays the foundation for physics-based inverse lithography in TPP.</jats:p>
title: Differentiable forward modeling and inverse lithography for two-photon lithography: application to voxel-by-voxel, diffractive optical element, and spatial light modulator systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>We present a comprehensive study of pitch 20 nm (P20) and pitch 18 nm (P18) metal logic designs, including regular tip-to-tip (T2T) and logic structures using bright-field masks in combination with dry metal-oxide resist. Patterning performance is evaluated across multiple source configurations and resist process conditions. For P20 T2T, we demonstrate a ∼13 nm T2T-CD (critical dimension) with local CD uniformity (LCDU) below 3 nm. For P18, single high-NA EUV exposure enables 18 nm T2T-CD with LCDU<3 nm. Further scaling is achieved using a directional etch at resist, reducing T2T-CD to ∼9 nm while maintaining LCDU ∼3 nm in P18 structure. To assess manufacturability, large-area defectivity is investigated using e-beam inspection after etch into hardmask for P20 metal logic structures. These results demonstrate the feasibility of single-patterning approaches for advanced metal logic and support the adoption of High-NA EUV for damascene integration.</jats:p>
title: Enabling single-exposure metal logic with high-NA lithography

items.abstract: <jats:p>Deep reactive ion etching (Bosch process) is a core technology in silicon microfabrication; however, its performance is still limited by outline defects, such as bottom corner height differences. We systematically investigated the influence mechanism of the aforementioned parameters on the bottom-of-trench etching flatness by solely regulating key process parameters during the passivation layer deposition (C4F8) and etching (SF6) stages. These parameters included gas flow rates, time ratios, and bottom radio frequency power. Throughout the process, no other gases, such as chlorine-based gases, were introduced. Only these two gases were employed for process adjustment. Experimental results indicate that optimal bottom flatness is achieved with a C4F8 flow rate of 150 to 350 sccm, an SF6 flow rate of 500 sccm, a passivation/etching time ratio of 1.12:1, and a bottom radio frequency (RF) power of 100 W. In addition, findings reveal that increasing the C4F8 time significantly enhances bottom height differences; increasing the SF6 flow rate initially decreases height differences before causing them to rise again; and bottom RF power below 80 W induces micro-mask effects, whereas power levels above 120 W exacerbate height differences, with 100 W identified as the equilibrium point. We quantify the critical process window, providing a theoretical foundation and process pathways for achieving high-precision control over silicon etching morphology.</jats:p>
title: Regulation of silicon bottom corner flatness through multi-parameter collaborative optimization in deep reactive ion etching

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundAs semiconductor device scaling progresses into the sub-10 nm critical-dimension regime, the adoption of extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography for high-volume manufacturing (HVM) of advanced nodes has brought stochastic variability and its resulting failures to the forefront of yield-loss concerns. EUV photons possess high energy, complicating absorption by photoresists and exacerbating random defectivity as feature sizes shrink. Although continuous improvements have been made in photoresist performance, mask technology, and post-lithography processes, stochastic defects remain a major source of yield loss in HVM. Experimental approaches for identifying, analyzing, and correcting stochastic defectivity are costly, requiring large numbers of wafers, extensive metrology resources, and considerable time.AimWe discuss a cost-effective predictive failure probability model (FPM) and demonstrate that it is an essential tool for studying and reducing stochastic defectivity in EUVL.ApproachBy leveraging rigorous probabilistic computational lithography methods, we construct accurate EUVL failure probability models. We use actual defect inspection tools to show how many more defects can be detected using the FPM’s predicted hotspots or weak points (WPs) compared with a conventional WP detection method.ResultsOur results confirm that the defectivity predictions generated by the FPM are in good agreement with e-beam inspection measurements. Larger-area inspection of space bridge defects was performed with optical defect inspection tools. In this case, defect detection was enhanced by use of FPM predictive simulation: defect detection using FPM output was 1.48× higher versus the standard methods.ConclusionBy leveraging FPMs grounded in rigorous probabilistic computational lithography, we are able to make robust predictions of stochastic defectivity over large layout areas, thereby establishing an optimal patterning process.</jats:p>
title: Computational lithography for large-area stochastic hotspot prediction and improved detection performance

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundMultipatterning (MPT) technology is a class of technologies for integrated circuit (IC) manufacturing to make the density of features of a layer beyond the limitations of a single exposure lithography. As the semiconductor process further scales down to 2 nm and beyond, the MPT technology has emerged as the clear choice for the routing of metal layers even within the era of extreme ultraviolet lithography. The stitching technique within MPT can divide a node into multiple nodes, each of which can be assigned to different colors to prevent color conflicts. This stitching approach is essential for resolving the m-coloring problem in the real-world patterning process without increasing the number of masks or adding chip-area penalties. As the chip manufacturing process continues to shrink, triple and quadruple patterning technologies (TPT/QPT), along with automatic stitching solution, become more and more worthwhile for chip scaling. However, as the complexity of IC design escalates, identifying the optimal stitching locations for the congested routing metal layers becomes increasingly challenging.AimSynopsys IC Validator (ICV) provides a complete and integrated flow of TPT/QPT, featuring an innovative stitching methodology.ApproachThe stitching flow consists of three key steps. Step 1 (stitch generation): generating possible effective stitches after color conflicts are detected in the initial coloring. Step 2 (link mapping): identifying spaces less than the minimum coloring distance with these stitch candidates. Step 3 (re-coloring with stitch candidates): selecting and applying valid stitches among all stitch candidates to obtain TPT/QPT-compliant layouts.ResultsICV’s stitching flow for TPT/QPT has demonstrated its effectiveness in managing the dense routing metal layers of the most advanced logic technology. By employing this sophisticated and integrated approach, we can achieve stringent chip-scaling targets while maintaining acceptable routing and coloring turnaround times. Finally, our proposed stitching solution can be seamlessly extended to more complex patterning technologies with a larger number of exposure masks (i.e., five, six masks, …), as needed.ConclusionsIn summary, ICV’s stitching technology for the MPT lithography is a valuable and efficient solution for automatic layout-fixing and engineering change order (ECO) routing, ensuring high-quality results in the most advanced logic designs.</jats:p>
title: Automatic stitching solution for multipatterning compliant routing metal layers beyond 2 nm

items.abstract: <jats:p>The semiconductor industry is a critical enabler of the digital economy, yet its manufacturing processes are among the most greenhouse gas (GHG)-intensive in the industrial sector, particularly due to process emissions from high global warming potential (GWP) gases such as perfluorocarbons , nitrogen trifluoride (NF3), and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6). Although abatement technologies and process optimization have reduced emissions intensity, persistent challenges in data granularity, timeliness, and interoperability limit the effectiveness of reduction strategies. This paper elaborates an integrated process GHG data visibility framework for the semiconductor industry, leveraging advanced sensing, real-time analytics, and cross-platform data integration to capture accurate, process-level emissions data. By enabling greater transparency, the framework creates opportunities for predictive abatement planning, AI-assisted process optimization, precise Scope 1 reporting, and many more. Case scenarios demonstrate how improved data visibility can accelerate the industry’s path toward net-zero goals while fostering competitive advantages through operational efficiency and environmental leadership.</jats:p>
title: From data to decarbonization: enhancing process greenhouse gas visibility in semiconductor manufacturing

items.abstract: <jats:p>For over five decades, reactive ion etching (RIE) has been a foundational technique in the semiconductor industry, enabling the high-throughput fabrication of countless wafers. Its effectiveness stems from the synergistic interaction between reactive chemical species and highly energized ions, which has underpinned the advancement of modern microelectronics. However, as device architectures become increasingly complex—with reduced feature sizes and high-aspect-ratio 3D structures—conventional RIE faces significant limitations. The traditional ion-chemical synergy becomes less effective, leading to reduced etching efficiency and throughput. To overcome these challenges, cryogenic plasma etching using hydrogen fluoride (HF)-containing species has emerged as a promising approach, leveraging a unique interplay between ions, physisorbed surface species, and substrate materials. A mini overview is provided for cryogenic plasma etching in SiO2 and SiN, specifically for NAND flash memory applications. As part of this review, the etching mechanisms of HF-based cryogenic plasma etching are discussed on the basis of plasma diagnostics and surface-structure analyses. Finally, the outlook and prospects for cryogenic RIE are also discussed.</jats:p>
title: Cryogenic plasma etching for SiO2/SiN dielectric films: a mini review

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundContinued device scaling beyond high numerical aperture (NA) EUV (NA=0.55) resolution motivates the exploration of “hyper-NA” EUV lithography systems (NA≥0.75), which promise improved contrast and resolution but introduce stronger mask 3D effects, increased polarization sensitivity, and reduced depth of focus (DoF).AimWe assess whether 0.75 NA EUV can provide manufacturable imaging for post-2030 logic interconnect patterning and identify the principal ecosystem constraints on masks, depth of focus, and photoresists.ApproachWe analyze the consequences of NA scaling on the EUV scanner architecture, including mask-side angle distributions, and we model multilayer and absorber effects. Imaging performance is quantified through rigorous simulations with source mask optimization (SMO), comparing 0.55 and 0.75 NA under unpolarized illumination and central-obscuration constraints. Two representative use cases are studied: (i) a CFET Metal0 (M0) layer with 16-nm pitch lines/spaces and line-end structures, and (ii) 2D interconnect blocks down to 16-nm pitch. Photoresist effects are included via a simplified blur and absorption model, and local EPE tail behavior is assessed using ±20% dose contours with NA-scaled defocus.ResultsModest multilayer period adjustments are sufficient to support the larger mask-side angles at 0.75 NA with limited average reflectivity impact, while low-n/high-k mask absorbers improve contrast and reduce mask-3D penalties relative to standard Ta-based absorbers. Hyper NA consistently increases the image log slope (ILS)—with the largest gains observed for dark-field masks on the most critical CFET interconnect features—and reduces local EPE extremes compared with 0.55 NA in the evaluated patterns. The Rayleigh DoF at 0.75 NA decreases to ∼20 nm, indicating the need for thinner resist films and improved focus/wafer topography control.ConclusionsUnder the modeled assumptions, 0.75 NA hyper-NA EUV offers significant contrast and EPE-tail improvements for CFET-relevant interconnect layers without revealing fundamental imaging limitations, provided that mask multilayer/absorber optimization, scanner focus control, and thin-film resist performance advance in a coordinated manner.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundNonchemically amplified resists (n-CARs) have emerged as a promising candidate for the next-generation of resists. Sulfonium-based n-CARs exhibit the capability of forming patterns with high resolution and low LER. However, their practical application is severely hindered by the low sensitivity.AimIt is expected to improve the sensitivity of sulfonium-based n-CARs by enhancing the absorption of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) or electron irradiation, thereby increasing the yield of secondary electrons and promoting the subsequent chemical reactions.ApproachFluorine has a higher EUV absorption cross-section than that of carbon and oxygen elements. Introduction of F-C bonds to resist matrix will boost the EUV photons or electrons absorption and induce the occurrence of new photochemical reactions. items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundIn integrated circuit manufacturing, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) has long served as the golden reference for optical critical dimension (OCD) measurement. However, the reliability of TEM data is frequently challenged by the sample destructive preparation, and subjective human interpretation is usually affects by the boundary selection between features in the TEM measurement. Such TEM reference uncertainty will introduce significant challenges when tuning the OCD models based on the reference data, thereby compromising the OCD measurement accuracy.AimThis work proposes a framework designed to systematically validate the TEM data, reduce the TEM measurement uncertainty, and thereby enhance OCD measurement accuracy.ApproachA comprehensive TEM-reference diagnostic framework was developed, integrating optimized TEM sampling, machine learning-based Auto-TEM measurement, statistical regression diagnostics using Cook’s distance and standardized residual analysis, and machine learning sensitivity analysis based on a leave-one-out strategy. The framework was validated using SiGe etch structures in a 28 nm planar process flow.ResultsThe optimized sampling strategy and Auto-TEM workflow reduced random and operator-induced variability in TEM reference extraction. Regression diagnostics identified abnormal TEM reference sites that strongly affected the OCD–TEM calibration. After excluding these unreliable references, the conventional model-based OCD calibration improved, with R2 increasing from 0.76 to 0.86 and the calibration slope changing from 0.76 to 0.82. The ML-based OCD workflow independently identified the same abnormal reference sites through leave-one-out sensitivity analysis. After reference screening, the ML-based correlation improved from R2=0.77 to 0.88, with the regression slope changing from 1.09 to 1.18. These results indicate that abnormal TEM reference data can introduce systematic OCD-to-TEM calibration errors on the order of 10%.ConclusionsThe results demonstrate that the integrity of TEM reference data should be explicitly evaluated rather than assumed a priori in OCD calibration workflows. The proposed framework effectively reduces both systematic and random uncertainty originating from TEM measurements, thereby improving OCD calibration robustness and model reliability. In addition, the Auto-TEM workflow further suppresses operator-induced variability and enables more stable reference extraction for advanced-node OCD metrology.</jats:p>
title: Improving optical critical dimension metrology via systematic screening of TEM reference data

items.abstract: <jats:p>As semiconductor patterning complexity continues to escalate, the early identification of latent weak patterns has become increasingly critical for maintaining yield stability and controlling metrology cost. Conventional identification strategies—primarily based on rule libraries, simulation heuristics, or limited sampling—often lack sufficient coverage and fail to provide statistically reliable assessments of defect vulnerability. The recent availability of production-scale wafer measurement data presents a fundamental opportunity to shift weak-pattern discovery from heuristic screening toward statistically grounded risk modeling. However, transforming such large-volume manufacturing data into actionable insights remains challenging due to feature heterogeneity, data redundancy, and limited interpretability of existing approaches. To address this gap, we introduce a wafer-driven vulnerability quantification framework that enables statistically robust weak-pattern discovery at production scale. Multidomain features derived from design geometry and computational lithography are integrated with over four million real wafer measurements to classify pattern populations and quantify defect risk at the cluster level. Unlike prior clustering-based layout classification studies, the proposed approach performs clustering using design-derived features, whereas wafer measurement data are subsequently integrated at the cluster level to enable statistically grounded risk-based prioritization. Evaluations conducted on production datasets demonstrate that the framework successfully identifies both previously known and undiscovered weak-pattern groups while substantially improving sampling reliability. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first production-scale study that integrates wafer measurement data with unsupervised clustering for statistically grounded weak-pattern ranking. Weak pattern discovery is inherently an unsupervised structural grouping problem as defect-prone configurations are not known a priori and labeled datasets are rarely available in production environments. In addition, a cluster-level visualization methodology enhances engineering interpretability and supports faster decision-making. Collectively, the proposed approach establishes a scalable, manufacturing-aware paradigm for data-driven metrology planning and weak-pattern discovery in advanced semiconductor processes. This design-first and data-augmented strategy ensures generalizability to unseen layouts while leveraging wafer data for statistically reliable vulnerability assessment.</jats:p>
title: Wafer-data augmented unsupervised clustering for weak-pattern detection in advanced semiconductor manufacturing

items.abstract: <jats:p>Free-electron lasers offer the capability to generate light with any property or quality as well as power/brightness required by the end-user/application. For decades, this technology has been developed by universities and national labs around the world for scientific applications and a few industrial/military demonstrations. Now, both the necessary particle accelerator ecosystem [e.g., superconducting radio frequency (RF), electron guns, undulators, solid-state RF amplifiers, and cryogenics] and free-electron laser expertise have reached a maturity where industrialization is possible for high-energy systems. The advantages for the semiconductor industry are in lithography (lower cost, improved k1, better edge-placement error), metrology (new nondestructive techniques, higher sampling, improved resolution) and inspection (faster, higher sensitivity, material specific). Although each of these critical functions could benefit from utilizing a free-electron laser, the economics and disruption of introducing these capabilities shape the reality of establishing new, “utility-scale” infrastructure in factories central to modern society.</jats:p>
title: Industrialized free-electron lasers: utility-scale light source readiness for semiconductor manufacturing

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundWith the continuous scaling down of integrated circuit feature sizes, the mismatch between the resolution of lithography systems and the feature dimensions leads to undesired shape distortions in wafer imaging, which can cause circuit malfunctions. These distorted regions are referred to as lithography hotspots (LHSs). Therefore, hotspot detection is crucial for ensuring the manufacturability and yield of integrated circuits.AimWe aim to develop a high-performance hotspot detection framework that enhances feature representation, reduces false alarms, and accelerates inference. It addresses the limitations of existing methods in detecting complex and fine-grained hotspot patterns under advanced process nodes.ApproachWe propose a re-parameterizable deep layer aggregation network that employs deep layer aggregation (DLA) to iteratively and hierarchically fuse multi-level features for improved hotspot recognition. The backbone integrates re-parameterizable convolutional blocks to speed up inference, whereas a multi-scale triple fusion (MSTF) module is introduced to further strengthen multi-scale feature integration.ResultsWe evaluated our method on standard LHS benchmarks. It outperforms state-of-the-art models in accuracy, false alarm reduction, and F1 score while cutting end-to-end runtime. Compared with prior approaches, our method shows measurable gains across all key metrics. Specifically, it delivers notable improvements in both detection performance and efficiency.ConclusionsThe proposed DLA-based re-parameterizable architecture offers an effective and efficient approach for detecting LHSs, improving both accuracy and computational efficiency. We point to a practical direction for design that considers manufacturability and could be extended to future studies on hotspot prediction in emerging technology nodes and more complex patterning processes.</jats:p>
title: Re-parameterizable deep layer aggregation network for lithography hotspot detection

items.abstract: <jats:p>Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography is a cornerstone of next-generation computer chip patterning technologies, yet continued improvements in photoresist sensitivity and pattern fidelity are required to enable high-numerical-aperture EUV exposure tools. Numerous studies have shown that underlayers can significantly enhance EUV photoresist performance, including reduced dose-to-size and improved pattern quality. The physical and chemical mechanisms underlying these improvements remain incompletely understood. We investigate one such mechanism: the transport of the photo-acid generator (PAG) in an EUV photoresist–underlayer system. Using time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry depth profiling, we demonstrate that PAG molecules from an EUV chemically amplified resist penetrate significantly into a cross-linked siloxane underlayer. Through a series of experiments, we show that this penetration does not arise from secondary ion mass spectrometry knock-on artifacts, the underlayer already containing PAG-like additives in it or thermally enhanced diffusion. Instead, we find that PAG transport occurs during the spin-coating step at room temperature by the casting solvent. Complementary experiments further show that PAG initially loaded into the underlayer can be leached out by solvent during spin-coating. These results establish solvent-assisted small-molecule transport as a dominant mechanism governing photoresist–underlayer interactions and provide a mechanistic explanation for previously reported dose-to-size reductions for EUV photoresists.</jats:p>
title: Solvent-assisted transport of photo-acid generator in extreme ultraviolet photoresists and underlayers

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundSurface topology dictates many material qualities. In CMOS-compatible materials, roughened surfaces have been used to enhance solar cell efficiency, increase optical dispersion, and potentially enhance porous sensors and increase catalytic surface area. Techniques for roughening include wet etches, laser pulses, and standard reactive-ion etching (RIE). SU-8 n grass has been used as a roughening RIE mask.AimWe aim to develop a method to enhance the SU-8 n grass mask with the addition of a nickel thin film, and to optimize the thickness of this thin film for root-mean-squared (RMS) surface roughness on plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) SiO2 thin films.ApproachSU-8 nano grass was created on a SiO2 thin film by spin coating and etching in an oxygen plasma. The SU-8 grass was coated with varying thicknesses of nickel from 0 to 21 nm. The samples were etched in a CF4 plasma. The samples were characterized with an optical 3D profilometer, scanning electron microscope (including energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy to ensure removal of the nickel in the etch), and optical reflectance.ResultsNine nanometers of nickel resulted in an RMS surface roughness of 0.38 μm, 30 times rougher than with an SU-8 mask alone. Nickel thicknesses greater than 9 nm decreased roughness, likely due to the fragility of the features. Optical testing showed that samples etched with nickel had similar reflection characteristics despite their roughness differences.ConclusionNickel thin films on SU-8 nano grass assist in the etching of rough features from a reactive-ion etch. Nine nanometers of nickel were shown to produce the most roughness. This technique was done on PECVD SiO2 but has the potential to be applied to various semiconductors, insulators, and metals.</jats:p>
title: Metal-enhanced nanoscale surface roughening using nano grass etch masks

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundThe development in photolithography proceeds through multiple steps that require precise monitoring to capture each procedure. Although standard sensitivity analysis defines the static dose-to-clear endpoint, these conventional metrics fail to resolve the time-dependent physical and chemical pathways that dictate final pattern quality.AimWe aim to determine the effect of photoacid generator (PAG) loading and quencher additives on the sensitivity and time-resolved development pathways of a model chemically amplified photoresist exposed under extreme ultraviolet (EUV).ApproachInitial sensitivity analysis on silicon substrates established a dose-to-clear reference window for all resist formulations. Using this defined exposure range, a quartz crystal microbalance with resistance monitoring tracked real-time dissolution kinetics from low doses through full clearance in a diluted developer.ResultsDevelopment behavior was categorized into four distinct modes based on resonant frequency and motional resistance. Increasing PAG concentration or exposure dose systematically shifted the observed development behavior from diffusion-dominated uptake toward rapid bulk dissolution.ConclusionsSamples exhibiting similar final thicknesses can evolve through fundamentally distinct time-resolved development pathways. Here, we report a model photoresist formulation that transitions from swelling (at 5 wt.% PAG) to nonswelling behavior (at 10 and 20 wt.% PAG) during dissolution in a diluted developer. In addition, resists containing a photo-decomposable quencher required a higher exposure dose than their quencher-free counterparts to achieve similar dissolution behavior. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that real-time kinetic measurements are essential to capture the critical, transient interfacial states that govern EUV resist dissolution.</jats:p>
title: Effect of photoacid generator loading and quencher on development pathways in a model chemically amplified photoresist

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundUnderlayers (ULs) play a critical role in the performance of photoresist systems used in extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. Positioned between the resist and substrate, they influence adhesion, reflectivity, interfacial stability, and overall pattern fidelity. As EUV lithography progresses toward sub-10 nm patterning, the design and optimization of ULs have become increasingly important for mitigating stochastic effects. However, a comprehensive understanding of UL functionality is still lacking.AimOur goal is to develop a nondestructive methodology to characterize the chemical profile of underlayer materials, which is essential for understanding their functional role in EUV lithography.ApproachWe employ resonant soft X-ray reflectivity (RSoXR) near the carbon K-edge to quantitatively probe depth-dependent compositional variations in representative UL films. By tuning the X-ray energy across element-specific absorption edges, RSoXR with enhanced chemical contrast, enables direct observation of chemical heterogeneity within the underlayer.ResultsWe performed RSoXR measurements on spin-on glass (SOG) samples prepared under different curing conditions. A matrix-method algorithm was used to model the X-ray reflectivity and extract the corresponding optical constants and depth profiles. The simulated profiles indicate that the two curing methods result in different levels of curing uniformity, with light-cured SOGs exhibiting clear chemical heterogeneity.ConclusionsOur results highlight the capability of RSoXR to resolve subtle chemical variations in depth profile. This nondestructive metrology can be further extended to investigate EUV resists and UL-resist interfacial behavior, offering a comprehensive understanding of materials evolution throughout EUV lithography processes.</jats:p>
title: Unveiling chemical heterogeneity in underlayer materials via resonant soft X-ray reflectivity

items.abstract: <jats:p>Semiconductor integration is advancing toward increasingly three-dimensional structures, which elevates the importance of wafer hybrid bonding. In this process, Cu pads must be recessed by several nanometers to ensure proper bonding, requiring sub-nanometer measurement precision. We propose a method to efficiently evaluate Cu pad height using quad-detector backscattered-electron (BSE) signals integrated in the scanning electron microscopes (SEMs). We extracted surface-height information by analyzing signal differences from multiple directions. Using 350-nm-sized Cu pads, we confirmed sensitivity to height variation through comparison with atomic force microscopy. A repeatability test demonstrated a precision of 0.2 nm (3σ). The proposed method enables high-precision, high-throughput in-line metrology for hybrid bonding processes.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundThe molecular weight (MW) of a photoresist can influence its properties and is an important metric for patterning. However, it is challenging to measure the MW in the solid phase, where the spatial distribution of MW can be nonuniform due to segregation effects during deposition.AimUsing surface mass spectrometry techniques such as secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS); the ratio and abundance of characteristic secondary ions (SI) can be used to determine the MW of the polymer and potentially the spatial distribution of molecular weights.ApproachExperiments on polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) with different MW were analyzed with nanoprojectile SIMS (NP-SIMS) using Au4004+ as a primary ion and compared with reported values in the literature using different primary ion projectiles (Ga+, C60+, Au+).ResultsThe results are in good agreement with the literature. Using Au4004+ leads to a 5 to 100-fold increase in yields for observed PMMA peaks compared with other primary ions. We found that the sum of all ions between 0 and 200 m/z is inversely related to the MW of the polymer; however, factors related to manufacturing affect the yields significantly. A general trend of increasing MW and decreasing ratio of end-group to main chain ions was observed for all SIMS projectiles and could be applied to results obtained from different SIMS instrumentation. The experimental results were compared with theoretical end-group concentrations at the surface, and the equation for end-group segregation was fitted to the experimental values, which shows the influence of spin-casting compared with polymer melts in equilibrium.ConclusionNP-SIMS can be used to identify the MW of a sample if all other factors of the manufacturing process are carefully monitored. Furthermore, this method could be used to investigate the MW of as-cast photoresists or monitor changes in the MW of a polymer as a result of exposure. In addition, the detection of both main chain and end-group ions makes an analysis of the extent of surface segregation of end-groups feasible.</jats:p>
title: Secondary ion mass spectrometry on polymers: pathway to molecular weight determination and evaluation of surface segregation

items.abstract: <jats:p>The viability of next-generation extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography wavelengths is evaluated through photon–matter interactions across optical materials and photoresists, rather than by resolution scaling alone. Candidate wavelengths of 13.5, 11.3, 6.6, and 3.13 nm are examined within a unified materials-based framework to compare imaging capabilities, enabling assessment of wavelength-dependent tradeoffs. Photomask and optical multilayers impose primary constraints through refractive index contrast, absorption, dispersion, and achievable large-angle Bragg reflectance. Although 13.5 nm Mo/Si systems define the current baseline, 11.3 nm multilayers may provide improved index contrast, reduced absorption, and increased angular bandwidth, supporting more favorable optical performance. At shorter wavelengths, reduced index contrast and subnanometer layer thickness requirements may impose fundamental limits on reflectance, bandwidth, and manufacturability, which may challenge the practical implementation of 6.6 nm and water-window regimes. These limitations propagate to system behavior. Scatter-driven flare increases rapidly with decreasing wavelength, imposing stringent roughness requirements or motivating reduced-surface optical designs. Polarization effects may limit hyper-NA imaging at 13.5 nm, in which large incidence angles produce significant TE–TM imbalance and image contrast loss. Reduced numerical apertures at shorter wavelengths can mitigate polarization sensitivity, with 11.3 nm potentially providing a more favorable balance between angular performance and polarization behavior. Within the photoresist, increasing photon energy with shorter wavelengths produces higher-energy primary electrons and broader secondary-electron cascades, which can increase stochastic blur and offset optical resolution gains. This identifies new resist design opportunities based on core-level threshold matching, in which the exposure wavelength is aligned just above accessible core-level binding energies to constrain electron cascade transport. Wavelength–material pairings such as 11.3 nm with the Si L2,3 edge and 6.6 nm with the S L2,3 edge represent enabling photoresist opportunities to localize energy deposition and potentially reduce stochastic variability through control of electron dynamics rather than absorption alone. These results establish wavelength selection as a challenge of material convergence across multilayer optics, imaging physics, and photoresist response.</jats:p>
title: Evaluation of next generation EUV lithography wavelengths from material property perspectives

items.abstract: <jats:p>In high-NA and hyper-NA EUV lithography, the reduced depth of focus (DOF) necessitates the use of thin resist films. However, increasing the resist thickness is advantageous for improving the local critical dimension uniformity (LCDU) of contact-hole patterns. This creates an inherent trade-off between LCDU improvement during exposure and DOF control in the final resist pattern. To address this challenge, we propose a new material and process scheme in which the resist is maintained at a relatively large thickness during exposure to enhance LCDU, while the effective resist thickness is reduced after development by removing the defocused upper portion of the resist. We evaluated the feasibility of this concept using a chemically amplified resist (CAR) platform. We demonstrated a process using a 70 nm-thick CAR film followed by a 30 nm recess of the top resist region, resulting in an effective final resist thickness of ∼40 nm. The LCDU was approximately 4.41 nm for the conventional process using an initially coated 40 nm-thick resist film. In contrast, the LCDU improved to 3.67 nm when a 70 nm-coated resist was followed by the 30 nm resist-recess process. These results demonstrate the feasibility of controlled resist recessing as a practical approach for extending CAR-based contact hole patterning toward high-NA and hyper-NA EUV lithography.</jats:p>
title: Recessing material and process for improving contact hole patterns for high-NA and hyper-NA EUV lithography

items.abstract: <jats:p>Laser-based patterning in semiconductor manufacturing can suffer critical dimension (CD) distortion when heat diffuses beyond the intended pattern during exposure. We seek beam shape design settings that confine the thermal field within a target CD boundary for shaped beam pattern projection. A continuum mechanics computational framework solves transient heat diffusion under projected spatially uniform and nonuniform beam profiles. We then formulate cost functions that penalize CD deviation for above-threshold heating. A genetic algorithm optimizes beam intensity and pulse durations. For the nonuniform and uniform beams, the optimized minimum costs were 8.87·10−5 and 2.75·10−3, with above temperature threshold areas of 1.11·10−12 m2 and 1.33·10−12 m2, respectively. With 2% intensity fluctuations applied to the optimal uniform beam, critical dimension uniformity (CDU) improved by 57.1% when the fluctuations were skewed toward the lower bound of the GA-optimal intensity. Optimizing spatiotemporal beam delivery can reduce CD distortion and overheating, and the sensitivity to upward power drift motivates robust beam-control strategies for thermal-constrained patterning.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundHigh-numerical aperture (NA) extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography delivers superior resolution, but it severely restricts the depth of focus (DOF) window. To expand this margin, the detrimental impact of stray photons leaking into unexposed areas must be mitigated. Crucially, we confirmed that increasing the photo contrast to decrease stochastic failure conversely increases sensitivity to this leakage light, thereby degrading the DOF margin.AimWe aim to maximize the functional DOF window in the High-NA EUV process by understanding the effects of the photoresist material configurations and post-exposure bake (PEB) process conditions.ApproachBased on lithographic simulations, we employed a low-contrast resist environment that exhibits low sensitivity to optical leakage in defocused condition.ResultThe DOF window was expanded by elevating the PEB temperature, reducing the polymer molecular weight, decreasing the protecting group (PG) ratio, or applying a PG with high activation energy (Ea) for deprotection. These adjustments reduced profile degradation and pattern collapse by systematically lowering the photosensitivity of the resist matrix against optical leakage in High-NA process.ConclusionThese findings expose a fundamental problem of High-NA process. Widening the DOF margin requires an insensitive resist environment, which can inherently degrade pattern uniformity. Therefore, achieving a manufacturing window demands a multidimensional approach that precisely balances process margin with stochastic problem.</jats:p>
title: Balancing DOF margin and stochastic failure in high-NA EUV process

items.abstract: <jats:p>Because generating realistic synthetic scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images remains a challenge in microelectronics, we used a deep learning approach to address this. A residual model based on convolutional Variational Autoencoders (ResCVAE) was trained using binary image patches of layouts. Our work has shown that our ResCVAE is able to promptly generate realistic synthetic SEM images, reproducing 1D and 2D postetch patterns. Moreover, SEM texture can be reproduced using the discrete wavelet transform.</jats:p>
title: Modeling the full process from layout to postetch imaging using a variational autoencoder

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundIn extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, low-n masks can provide increased contrast. However, they suffer from M3D phase effects for isolated structures when using dark field imaging. These lead to the best focus offsets between different features. Simulations have shown that patterning the absorber with SRGs mitigates this. Consequently, the best foci are aligned, and image distortion is reduced. Aligning best foci is of critical importance for hyper NA imaging as the depth-of-focus decreases with increasing NA.AimShow experimentally that the proposed sub-resolution gratings work as intended for dark-field imaging.ApproachAnalyze wafers printed with a low-n mask containing sub-resolution gratings.ResultsSub-resolution gratings work as intended. The best focus of isolated lines and spaces is aligned with the best focus of dense lines and spaces. The CD asymmetry through the focus of two neighboring trenches (2 bar), a standard feature to showcase M3D effects, can be mitigated if it is surrounded by SRGs.ConclusionsSRGs can mitigate M3D effects for low-n masks in dark-field imaging and enhance the overlapping depth-of-focus.</jats:p>
title: Experimental verification of sub-resolution grating on a low-n mask using high-NA extreme ultraviolet lithography

items.abstract: <jats:p>Line-edge roughness (LER) has become a dominant contributor to critical-dimension variability as lithographic features approach the nanometer scale. Although scanning electron microscopy (SEM) remains the workhorse tool for roughness monitoring, SEM-based LER values are susceptible to noise bias, digitization artifacts, and limited spatial-frequency bandwidth. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) provides a geometry-based alternative by directly measuring topography, but AFM-based LER is likewise sensitive to analysis choices, particularly edge definition, effective resolution, probe convolution, and statistical treatment of correlated samples. Here, we propose a practical framework for quantitative AFM-based LER metrology of lithographic line/space patterns. Two complementary edge definitions are compared: a height-threshold method that evaluates roughness at the same relative height used for critical-dimension extraction and a model-based edge definition in which the edge is assigned to the center of an error-function transition, corresponding to the maximum gradient. We show analytically that the height-threshold method at threshold=0.5 is geometrically consistent with the error-function center for approximately symmetric transitions, and we demonstrate that this agreement is reflected experimentally for the present poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) patterns. Using electron-beam-lithographed PMMA patterns, we further examine effective pixel size through a convergence study and report LER together with confidence intervals derived from an effective sample size estimated from the correlation length. For 250 nm half-pitch patterns, repeated measurements across ten sites yield coefficients of variation below 6%. In this dataset, measured LER plateaus when the effective pixel size is reduced below about 1 to 2 nm/pixel; this result is used as an experimental convergence criterion rather than as a universal probe-resolution prescription. Cross-validation against an independent in-house workflow shows that agreement between software packages is achieved only after the edge is explicitly defined. The proposed framework provides a practical route to reproducible AFM-based LER values and uncertainty reporting, and it complements existing SEM-centered roughness protocols by introducing AFM-specific criteria.</jats:p>
title: Robust and standardized framework for quantitative AFM-based line-edge roughness metrology of lithographic line/space patterns

items.abstract: <jats:p>Metal oxide resists (MORs) have shown great promise for high-resolution patterning in extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, with potential for integration into high-volume manufacturing. However, MORs have recently been shown to exhibit sensitivity to process conditions and environment, leading to critical dimension (CD) variation. Although this variation can be reduced with proper process control, there is a current lack of fundamental knowledge on how these aspects affect the pattern formation mechanism. Moreover, the diverse composition of atmospheric environments makes it difficult to disentangle the role of individual atmospheric components on the lithographic performance of this promising class of EUV photoresists. To bridge these knowledge gaps, we deploy a coordinated, fundamentals-focused approach to yield deep insights into MOR exposure and process chemistry. Our results on a model MOR, an n-butyl Sn-Ox system, reveal how parameters such as exposure dose, post-exposure bake (PEB) temperature, and atmospheric environment influence the EUV exposure and post-exposure delay (PED) and PEB mechanisms. Using an advanced toolset, we show that EUV-induced ligand cleavage likely occurs via homolytic Sn–C bond breaking, resulting in a Sn-based radical “active site,” which serves as a reactive center that endows MOR materials with their sensitivity to atmospheric components (e.g., H2O and O2) during PED and PEB. We resolve the roles of H2O during PED and PEB, and in particular, we show that PEB environments containing O2 exhibit increased litho performance (reduced dose and improved development contrast), suggesting that O2 plays a critical role in the exposure and thermal mechanisms of MOR materials. Our results, and the coordinated approach using correlative spectroscopies, provide a strong foundation for understanding the critical EUV exposure and PED and PEB mechanisms in MOR materials, provide insights into potential optimization routes via environmental control during the process, and finally offer the potential to link mechanistic aspects and MOR lithographic performance and stability.</jats:p>
title: Fundamental understanding of exposure and process chemistry of Sn-based metal oxide resists: effects of ambient environment during post-exposure delay and bake

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundEnsuring high yields in semiconductor manufacturing requires rigorous defect detection. However, in the context of machine learning, supervised methods rely on manually annotated datasets of scanning electron microscope (SEM) images, which are expensive and labor-intensive to acquire.ObjectiveTo overcome this data scarcity, particularly for “rare event” defects, we propose a reconstruction-based defect-detection framework driven by generative diffusion models.MethodsA denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) was trained exclusively on defect-free synthetic SEM images generated with controlled contact-edge roughness, critical-dimension variability, edge-intensity effects, and electron-beam and instrument noise. During inference, a partially noised input image was reconstructed with a denoising diffusion inference model sampling procedure toward the learned clean-image manifold. Defects were localized from residual heatmaps between the input and reconstructed image, followed by adaptive thresholding and connected-component area scoring. The method was evaluated against cell-to-cell (C2C), autoencoder, and latent diffusion baselines, with additional sensitivity, robustness, and stress-test analyses.ResultsOn the synthetic test set, the DDPM achieved the highest performance, followed by Latent DDPM. C2C also performed strongly, but DDPM showed improved performance in stress cases with multiple defects and variable hole sizes, where repeated-cell reference assumptions were weakened. Both diffusion models showcased stability in seed and noise-ratio sensitivity analysis, with DDPM showing more consistency but longer inference time, although comparable to C2C and latent DDPM in this evaluation setting. A qualitative illustration using four real SEM examples showed nominal-pattern reconstruction and localization of one visible merged-hole defect.ConclusionWithout defect labels for reference generation or model training, this approach helps address a major bottleneck in quality control; only the final decision threshold is calibrated using labeled simulated validation data.</jats:p>
title: Reconstruction-based generative diffusion framework for label-free defect detection in SEM images of contact-hole arrays

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundAs the semiconductor industry pushes the boundaries of extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUVL) for advanced node semiconductor chips, the performance of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) photoresists (PRs) becomes increasingly critical in determining patterning resolution and overall chip quality. However, traditional evaluation methods for EUV PR patterning performance are struggling to keep pace with tightening scales, necessitating innovative approaches.AimTo this end, we propose a three-dimensional (3D) cliff analysis method that leverages after development inspection scanning electron microscopy images to visualize and quantify EUV PR resolution in three-dimensional ways.ApproachThis approach enables the precise characterization of stochastic failure defects such as bridge/break and missing/merging, offering unprecedented insights into PR performance based not only on the dose but also on the focus metrics.ResultsThis 3D cliff analysis method is applicable to both line/space and contact/hole patterns and can be used to assess not only defects but also other factors such as line width roughness and local critical dimension uniformity (LCDU).ConclusionsOur results demonstrate that the 3D cliff analysis method provides a comprehensive understanding of EUV PR behavior, enabling the optimization of patterning processes and improved chip yields. This approach has the potential to significantly enhance the development of EUVL and contribute to the advancement of high numerical aperture EUVL.</jats:p>
title: Three-dimensional cliff analysis method for defining patterning resolution in EUV lithography

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Advanced semiconductor logic nodes have shifted toward gate-all-around (GAA) architectures, such as Nanosheet, Forksheet, and complementary field-effect transistor devices. This shift has imposed more stringent measurement requirements at the front-end-of-line process stages. As the GAA architecture has been advanced to improve device performance, power efficiency and reduce device dimensions, the complexity in structural design and material integration is observed. A fundamental limit in structural characterization for GAA devices has been reached by conventional metrology, primarily due to the intricate 3D, high-aspect-ratio vertical stacked channels with buried nanoscale features.Aim: To address these complexities and support process control, several metrologies are reviewed, with an emphasis on X-ray metrology and the inclusion of other relevant metrologies.Review Approach: Recent developments in metrology are discussed in detail. Analysis is focused on measurement configurations, in-line applicability, and advancements aligned with the demands of next-generation logic nodes.Conclusion: The correspondence between X-ray metrology advancements and architecture-driven requirements is evaluated in this review. X-ray metrology developments are assessed for the potential to facilitate the characterization of 3D nanoscale features within future logic device fabrication.</jats:p>
title: X-ray metrology for advanced semiconductor manufacturing of next-generation logic devices

items.abstract: <jats:p>To achieve finer feature sizes and enhanced imaging resolution, semiconductor lithography continuously pursues shorter exposure wavelengths and increased numerical aperture (NA). At the same time, the depth of focus (DoF) inevitably decreases. Simulations and initial experiments show that the introduction of high-NA extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography will lead to 2.5–3X DoF reduction compared with low-NA EUV. With the introduction of high-NA EUV, it is thus expected that focus control will become increasingly critical for achieving the desired pattern fidelity. We describe the results of our scanning electron microscope–based focus metrology method. We describe optimization of our methodology as well as its sensitivity to data collection parameters. Next, we explore the effects of wafer topography in printing results for a low-NA EUV exposure of a 32-nm minimum pitch logic pattern. We use programmed topography to mimic that of a full-loop logic device. Multiple programmed heights are evaluated and densely placed metrology structures are used for focus metrology. Finally, we show how the presence of topography reduces pattern fidelity and introduces defects.</jats:p>
title: Wafer topography impact on focus and defectivity with enhanced method for EUV focus metrology
container-title: Journal of Micro/Nanopatterning, Materials, and Metrology

items.abstract: <jats:p>We propose a simple, four-mirror, in-line projector for high-NA EUV lithography that eliminates the most troublesome mask 3D effect. The design consists of a two-stage concave-convex pair, where optical aberrations are canceled within each stage and between them, in a manner similar to that of the double-Gauss lens. The light rays pass through the central aperture in each mirror with acceptable obscuration. The numerical aperture is 0.5 and 0.55. It has a circular exposure field with a diameter of 20 and 30 mm, respectively. The residual radial distortion is rather high at a few microns at the field rim, and the scan motion causes image blurring in the scanner. Thus, we need to revert to the stepper design, and the field becomes smaller, i.e., 14 mm×14 mm square and 21×21 mm. However, we can remove the scanning mechanism from the photomask side; thus, it makes the system simple. It is important to note that both the wafer and the photomask remain stationary during the EUV exposure. Illumination will be provided through two rectangular scan-mirrors located in front of the mask, providing dual line scan field, which matches with off-axis illumination enhancing the resolution and bypassing the central obscurations.</jats:p>
title: High-NA in-line projector for EUV lithography

items.abstract: <jats:p>Per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) have come under increased scrutiny because all members of this class of compounds exhibit very high environmental persistence (vP), and some exhibit toxicity (T) and/or bioaccumulation (B) potential. Because of these attributes, PFAS chemicals are being scrutinized by regulatory authorities for restrictions on use and releases to the environment. At the same time, PFAS are crucial components of many process materials used in semiconductor photolithography, to the extent that the manufacture of advanced chips is currently not possible without them. Although PFAS uses are crucial, the amounts used in these key applications are small relative to global PFAS production and use, a fact that may not be generally known. Our purpose is to provide a quantitative assessment of the amount of PFAS used in semiconductor photolithography and to present a mass balance model for the disposition of these materials into applicable waste streams. The model presented allows identification of key areas for prioritized action, including the need for targeted research and development.</jats:p>
title: PFAS in semiconductor photolithography: a mass balance model
container-title: Journal of Micro/Nanopatterning, Materials, and Metrology

items.abstract: <jats:p>In advanced technology nodes, optical proximity correction (OPC) solutions employ a blend of rules-based and model-based treatments to correct the intended circuit design. Rules-based OPC (RB-OPC) is based on a table or series of tables that prescribe discrete treatments for a feature as a function of its surrounding environment. RB-OPC is typically utilized for applications such as etch-bias compensation, silicon process-bias definition, and OPC model correction. One drawback to defining a rules-based table (RBT) is that the empirical measurements used to populate the table are typically sparse in terms of feature size and pitch, requiring the OPC engineer to fully populate the RBT by other means. Rather than manually interpolating the RBT, scattered-data interpolation techniques could be used to automatically populate the RBT at the desired level of granularity. Scattered data interpolation is commonly used in applications such as meteorology and terrain cartography as it relies on unevenly distributed sparse sample points to characterize the behavior of an entire region. In this study, the proposed technique was applied to correct optical OPC model error on a 28-nm implant level and compared with the baseline process, which uses an empirically calibrated OPC model. XOR analysis confirmed that the desired RB-OPC treatments were applied after optical OPC model correction for one-dimensional features, but two-dimensional features require independent characterization and correction. Experimental results also demonstrated comparable performance between the baseline empirical OPC model and variants of RB-OPC treatment, as all methods resulted in patterns with a global root mean square percentage error between 11% and 12%. The next steps of this study include testing applications in etch bias characterization, as well as testing alternative interpolation methods.</jats:p>
title: Automating rules-based optical proximity correction via scattered data interpolation

items.abstract: <jats:p>We present innovative design strategies to eliminate the need for at-resolution field stitching in high-numerical aperture extreme ultraviolet lithography. For logic applications, two complementary approaches at the inter- and intra-cell levels are proposed. These include the insertion of dummy filler cells or relaxed-pitch cells, combined with metal routing blockages, which can be seamlessly implemented within a modified place-and-route flow, thereby simplifying process complexities associated with at-resolution stitching. For dynamic random access memory applications, a die aspect ratio optimization methodology is introduced to maximize mask area utilization and improve manufacturing throughput. Depending on the die arrangement in the full imaging field, two stitching scenarios are identified: an even number of dies in the Y-direction, enabling pitch-tolerant field stitching along the scribe lane, and an odd number of dies, which eliminates the need for critical-dimension-critical stitching at the stitching boundary.</jats:p>
title: Avoiding at-resolution stitching for logic and DRAM applications in high-NA EUV lithography

items.abstract: <jats:p>One of the challenges with high numerical aperture extreme ultra-violet lithography (high-NA EUVL) is the limited depth-of-focus (DOF). In this study, we demonstrate how an illumination source with the majority of pixels in the central obscuration region of the source can increase the process window of contact printing cases, especially in dynamic random access memory (DRAM) but also in logic applications, except in configurations with a center-to-center pitch smaller than ∼30 nm. We demonstrate this through full-resist model rigorous lithography simulations. For hexagonal contact configurations such as those used in DRAM, a simple qualitative explanation of the simulated DOF increase is also presented. An experimental validation of the simulated results will be presented in future work.</jats:p>
title: On the use of illumination-source pixels in the central-obscuration area for enhancing the process window of contact printing with high-NA EUV lithography

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundTin-based MOR resists are a high-performance type of EUV resist with mechanism is not well understood.AimThis work aims to provide a better understanding of how tin-based MOR resists operate.ApproachThe probability of cross-linking between adjacent nanoparticles was calculated. When that probability was over the bond percolation threshold the resist was considered exposed. This approach enables the calculation of dose to size and of exposure latitude (EL) based on resist parameters using spreadsheet calculations.ResultsSome molecular motion during the post exposure bake must be assumed in order to be predicted reasonable doses to print. Comparison of two reported literature values for electrons produced per photon (2.7 and 8) suggests that the lower value is correct. The conversion of tin ligands into cross linkable functional groups is likely not efficient, with many ligand loss events resulting in new functionality that does not cross-link.ConclusionsThere is molecular motion during the PEB of tin MOR resists that improves cross-linking efficiency and lowers the dose to size. The conversion efficiency of ligand loss events into functional groups that cross-link during PEB is less than 100% and could easily be as low as 50%. This suggests that additives that generate Sn-OH groups from radicals could be used to improve dose to print.</jats:p>
title: Probability modeling of tin-based MOR resists
