items.abstract: <jats:p>Photoresist patterning for semiconductor manufacturing is encountering new challenges with the move to extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, driven by smaller pitches, thinner resists, and fewer photons. Obtaining information about the nanoscale distribution of chemical changes in the resist will provide key information to optimize processing and resist development. Soft X-rays provide sensitivity to chemical functional groups at key atomic absorption edges, including carbon, oxygen, and fluorine. By conducting specular reflectivity measurements at these energies, we can track the chemical depth profiles in a resist. This process is demonstrated by characterizing the optical constant profiles, which are proportional to the concentration of chemical bonds in a film at soft X-ray energies, of an EUV resist coated on a cross-linked polystyrene (CLPS) mat. The resist was exposed to blanket exposures with different doses and measured at different stages of the process, including post-exposure but before the bake, after the post-exposure bake, and after development. Segregation of resist components was observed in the as-coated case films, with a fluorinated component aggregating at the film surface. Stratification of the chemical changes that occur in the film is observed after exposure, but before the bake. The magnitude of this stratification is dose-dependent. After a post-exposure bake, the stratification is no longer observed, and the optical constant profile is uniform with the exception of the fluorinated components. These results are complemented by near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy obtained with an imaging microscope. Finally, we also examine the CLPS mat before and after the process and observe evidence for chemical changes in the CLPS, with the possibility of residual resist components residing in the film after development.</jats:p>
title: Depth profiling chemical changes in chemically amplified resists for EUV lithography

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundThe semiconductor industry faces mounting pressure to improve energy efficiency and reduce environmental impact as device dimensions continue to shrink and patterning complexity increases. Thermal crosslinking of spin-on carbon (SOC) and spin-on glass (SOG) underlayers is a particularly energy-intensive step due to high temperature requirements.AimWe extend our previously reported optical crosslinking approach, replacing conventional thermal baking with a high-dose optical curing system, to both extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and argon fluoride immersion (ArFi) lithography. We also introduce per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS)-free underlayer formulations, designed to eliminate harmful fluorochemicals without sacrificing performance.ApproachComprehensive data on film crosslinking, lithographic performance, and energy savings are presented.ResultsOur optical crosslinking approach achieves energy savings of up to 85% for SOC and 60% for SOG in EUV processing and 75% and 60% for SOC and SOG, respectively, in ArFi processes. Furthermore, PFAS-free underlayers demonstrate competitive lithographic performance and robustness, comparable to conventional formulations.ConclusionsThese findings support a shift toward more sustainable semiconductor manufacturing by significantly reducing energy usage and eliminating environmentally harmful materials without compromising process performance.</jats:p>
title: Extension of optical crosslinking of EUV-compatible underlayers to PFAS-free and ArFi-compatible underlayers

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundAs extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography becomes essential for advanced semiconductor manufacturing, its increased hydrogen consumption presents a challenge to improve sustainability performance. Addressing hydrogen use is important to reduce environmental impact and strengthen supply chain resilience.AimWe evaluate the potential of hydrogen recycling systems (HRS) to lower the global warming impact of EUV lithography. It quantifies the general understanding of how circular hydrogen management can contribute to sustainable semiconductor production.ApproachA life cycle assessment (LCA) was conducted to compare four hydrogen abatement scenarios: combustion abatement, hydrogen dilution (H2D), HRS with combustion abatement, and HRS with H2D. Both embodied and indirect climate impacts of hydrogen were considered.ResultsImplementing HRS and H2D reduced global warming potential by up to 47% compared with combustion abatement. When combined with low-carbon electricity and hydrogen sourcing, reductions reached 80%. Although H2D appears favorable under the greenhouse gas protocol, the LCA results indicate that this is largely a consequence of GHGP’s exclusion of indirect hydrogen effects, underscoring how reporting methodology can substantially alter perceived climate impacts.ConclusionsHydrogen recycling reduces climate impact and reliance on virgin hydrogen and mitigates supply chain risks in EUV lithography. These findings support industry-wide decarbonization efforts and demonstrate the importance of integrating HRS into sustainable semiconductor manufacturing.</jats:p>
title: Global warming impact assessment of abatement systems for extreme ultraviolet lithography in wafer production: effect of hydrogen recycling and electricity sourcing

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundMetrology techniques with high accuracy and throughput are needed to address critical challenges in the characterization of periodic nanostructured materials. Copper interconnects are structures for which precise topography characterization is needed. Although common methods include atomic force and scanning electron microscopy, extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) scatterometry has unique capabilities for the characterization of structure parameters and material properties.AimWe study the effect of experimental design parameters (wavelength and incidence angle) on EUV scatterometry. We explore the fundamental sensitivity capabilities of EUV scatterometry for interconnect metrology when data are collected such that the information content in a single EUV diffraction pattern is maximized by tuning the wavelength and incidence angle.ApproachWe applied experimental design methods based on the Fisher information matrix to EUV scatterometry of an interconnect to obtain the optimized EUV wavelength and angles at which to obtain a single diffraction pattern. Using rigorous coupled wave analysis simulations and Monte Carlo uncertainty quantification, the accuracy of the parameter reconstructions under an optimal design is quantified.ResultsThe uncertainty of the sample parameters depends strongly on wavelength and incidence angle, necessitating experimental design methods to achieve maximal sensitivity. When data are collected under an optimal experimental design, simulations indicate that sub-angstrom accuracy can be obtained from only a single diffraction pattern for the dishing depth of interconnect pads (0.02 nm standard deviation), and the substrate density can additionally be extracted (0.015 g/cm3 standard deviation). Decorrelation of the sample parameters is observed with optimal design, and 13.8 nm EUV light provides better sensitivity than longer wavelengths such as 30 nm.ConclusionsExperimental design methods are an essential tool for ensuring that experimental data are collected under an optimal design that maximizes the information in the data. Implementing these methods opens further capabilities for fast and precise interconnect metrology with EUV scatterometry.</jats:p>
title: Optimizing experimental design for fast and accurate CD metrology of interconnects using coherent extreme-ultraviolet scatterometry

<jats:p>BackgroundInverse lithography technology (ILT) revolutionized computational lithography by offering significant advantages over traditional optical proximity correction through its capacity for complex mask shapes and robust gradient-based optimization.AimWe aim to propose and analyze the impact of a polar mask representation on ILT performance, evaluating it against existing mask representations using various optimization algorithms.ApproachWe investigate the polar coordinate representation for mask shapes, expressing them as a series expansion in polar coordinates. Its performance is compared with polygonal, Bezier multigonal, and level set representations within ILT, measuring the efficiency of pre-conditioning and various first-order gradient descent methods.ResultsThe polar coordinate approach demonstrates superior performance, characterized by faster convergence and reduced data volume, all while maintaining high accuracy. These improvements are attributed to mathematical properties that naturally align with common lithographic patterns, particularly for contact and via layers.ConclusionsThe polar approach offers a high-performance framework for ILT, providing rapid convergence and a compact, efficient representation for smooth mask morphologies, beneficial for contact-like layers.</jats:p>
title: Inverse lithography via polar representation for curvilinear mask synthesis

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundAs extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography advances toward sub-40-nm single-pattern pitches, stochastic defects have emerged as a critical barrier to pattern manufacturability. These rare patterning failures, such as line bridging or contact not-open, cannot be fully captured using conventional metrics including critical dimension (CD), line-edge roughness, and line-width roughness (LWR).AimWe aim to establish a quantitative framework for predicting stochastic defectivity by applying an extreme value statistical model to locally narrow space variations observed in EUV line–space patterns.ApproachMinimum space critical dimensions were extracted from critical-dimension scanning electron microscopy (CD-SEM) images and modeled using the Gumbel distribution derived from extreme value theory. The resulting stochastic defectivity D0 (defects/cm2) was compared with predictions based on the normal distribution. To evaluate the physical relevance of the model, Gumbel-based D0 values obtained from various published EUV resist images were correlated with pitch, dose-to-size (DtS), unbiased LWR, and Z-factor.ResultsThe Gumbel model predicted extreme tail defect probabilities several orders of magnitude higher than those estimated using a normal distribution, showing improved consistency with observed manufacturing limits. Pearson correlation analysis revealed strong dependence of D0 on pitch (r=−0.88) and unbiased LWR (r=+0.85), whereas Z-factor and DtS exhibited weak correlations.ConclusionsThese findings indicate that stochastic defectivity in EUV lithography is governed by extreme spatial gap fluctuations rather than by average process variation metrics. The proposed Gumbel-based D0 estimation provides a physically meaningful and practical indicator for assessing EUV pattern manufacturability, although further validation using large-area measurements is required.</jats:p>
title: Extreme value analysis of stochastic defects in extreme ultraviolet line-space patterns using the Gumbel distribution

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundHopkins’ transmission cross coefficient (TCC) formula is conventionally used in optical lithography simulations. In extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, the TCC formula must be modified to account for the mask 3D (M3D) effect of the thick EUV mask absorber. In the previous paper, we proposed the source-position-dependent TCC (STCC) formula, which used three TCCs (TCC, TCCSX, and TCCSY) to represent the source-position dependence of the M3D effect.AimThe polarization effect is not negligible in high-NA EUV lithography. The purpose of this work is to extend the STCC formula to include the polarization effect and enable accurate and fast simulation of polarization-dependent imaging in high-NA EUV lithography.ApproachTo include the polarization effect, an additional coherence function Cρ must be introduced into the STCC formula. Cρ represents the effect of the electric field rotation in the meridional plane, which depends on the polarization ρ=x or y.ResultsSix TCCs (TCCρ, TCCSXρ, and TCCSYρ) are required to include both the polarization and M3D effects in the STCC formula. For mask patterns with vertical lines, 18 TCCs are required.ConclusionsThe STCC formula is extended for high-NA EUV lithography simulations. The STCC formula is the basis of our convolutional neural network model, which accelerates EUV lithography simulations.</jats:p>
title: Source-position-dependent transmission cross coefficient formula including polarization and mask three-dimensional effects in high-numerical-aperture extreme ultraviolet lithography

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundPer- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are widely used in lithography materials because of their unique chemical and surface properties, but their extreme environmental persistence and toxicity drive increasing regulatory and sustainability pressure to eliminate their use. Substantial efforts are therefore underway to develop PFAS-free alternatives for photoresists and associated lithography materials across deep ultraviolet and extreme ultraviolet (EUV) technologies. However, an industry-wide visibility of the maturity of these PFAS-free solutions has been lacking.AimThis work aims to provide a transparent, technology-neutral snapshot of the maturity of PFAS-free lithography materials, including both photoresists and key ancillary materials, across major lithography platforms.ApproachAn anonymized lithographic materials supplier survey was conducted within a precompetitive framework using a lithography-adapted technology readiness level (TRL) scale ranging from TRL 1 to TRL 9. Participants self-assessed the maturity of their PFAS-free resists and ancillary materials for i-line, KrF, ArF dry, ArF immersion, and EUV lithography. All data were reported exclusively as aggregated TRL ranges to preserve confidentiality and avoid disclosure of proprietary or IP-sensitive information.ResultsPFAS-free resist solutions are reported for all lithography platforms, spanning TRLs 4 to 9. i-line and KrF resists show the highest readiness, including solutions approaching or reaching high-volume manufacturing. ArF dry, ArF immersion, and EUV resists are predominantly at mid-TRL levels, reflecting the ongoing performance optimization and integration work. Ancillary materials exhibit a wider dispersion in maturity, ranging from the topcoat category at TRLs 2 to 3 to PFAS-free developer rinses at TRL 9. The remaining gaps are largely driven by process integration, defectivity control, and manufacturing validation rather than fundamental chemical limitations.ConclusionsThe survey reveals that PFAS-free lithography materials are technically viable across the full lithography landscape. Although some platforms and material categories are close to manufacturing readiness, others, particularly EUV resists and selected ancillary materials, require further development. The anonymized, TRL-based assessment provides a common reference for the lithography community to prioritize R&D efforts toward fully PFAS-free lithographic manufacturing.</jats:p>
title: Technology readiness of PFAS-free lithography materials: an anonymized survey of resist and ancillary material maturity

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundImage-based overlay (IBO) target is a type of overlay metrology method in semiconductor manufacturing. Focus optimization is a critical factor that determines the quality of the IBO target signals in IBO target measurement. To calculate the overlay, two target images are required. As the semiconductor process becomes complex, optimizing the IBO target focus for both targets becomes increasingly difficult.AimWe target to develop a deep-learning-based method that tackles two issues in IBO target focus optimization. Instead of choosing a compromised focus offset for both targets or measuring different targets sequentially, we train a generative model that outputs IBO target images with different focus offsets. We use the model for the IBO target focus optimization.ApproachThe proposed method consists of two steps. The first step is to train a model; conditional deblurring network (cDN) generates IBO target images with different camera focus offsets. Our model is based on the deep image deblurring methods using the generative models with auxiliary focus offsets. The second step is to optimize IBO target images with the trained model. We can generate an optimal target image that consists of IBO target images with the best focus for each layer.ResultsIn experiments, we have compared different baseline models for cDN. The best model, which adopted DeblurGAN-v2, achieved a peak signal-to-noise-ratio of 49.04, a Fr’echet inception distance of 1.11, a mean squared error (MSE) of contrast precision of 0.0010, and an MSE of center-of-symmetry of 0.0672. The model can generate focus-adjusted IBO target images comparable to the ground truth. With the trained model, we optimized IBO target images. We achieved the improved target quality compared with the compromised best focus images.ConclusionsWe proposed a deep-learning-based methodology to solve the focus optimization problem for IBO target images. We demonstrated that our method can solve the IBO target optimization problem more efficiently than existing methods. In addition, we proved the applicability of deep learning in semiconductor manufacturing.</jats:p>
title: Focus enhancement for image-based overlay metrology targets via generative models

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundThe thermal deformation during dose accumulation shifts the image transfer path, leading to significant distortion in the local image profile. This phenomenon underscores the necessity of evaluating thermal deformation not merely as static placement errors but as factors affecting imaging performance.AimThis work aims to clarify how the thermal deformation occurring during EUV exposure directly influences image degradation and placement error.ApproachA thermomechanical wafer heating model is established to calculate transient deformation under EUV exposure. The resulting deformation data is subsequently coupled with lithography simulation results to calculate the local image profile. Finally, the image profile is analyzed to quantify the image twisting effect and placement error.ResultsPlacement errors exhibit spatially diverse distributions dependent on global field location and intra-slit coordinates. Furthermore, the dynamic variability of deformation during exposure was found to be a systematic source of image performance reduction, particularly through NILS reduction in fine-pitch patterns.ConclusionsThese results show that wafer deformation should be treated not only as a source of overlay error but also as a contributor to image degradation. This finding provides a basis for understanding deformation-induced placement error and image twisting in EUV lithography and for improving future overlay and imaging control strategies.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundStable and reproducible extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light generation is essential for advanced semiconductor lithography and actinic inspection. Conventional plasma-based EUV sources, such as laser-produced plasma and discharge-produced plasma, provide high output power but suffer from high power consumption, mirror contamination, electrode erosion, plasma instabilities, rapid optics degradation, and system complexity.AimWe (part I) focus on the design, long-term reliability, reproducibility, and operational stability of a vertically aligned carbon nanotube (CNT)-based cold electron-beam (C-beam)-driven EUV light source. The physical emission mechanism and source efficiency analysis are presented in the companion paper (part II).ApproachWe demonstrate a CNT cold cathode electron-beam (C-beam)-irradiated EUV source based on surface-excitation-driven EUV emission. The system operates at an optimized irradiation condition using a tin anode mounted on a copper jig, enabling controlled EUV generation while suppressing anode melting and cathode degradation.ResultsCompared with our previous lab measurements, the proposed C-beam EUV source exhibits a significant improvement in temporal stability. Short-term stability improved from 2.0% to 0.6%, whereas long-term stability improved from 4.0% to 2.5%. The source demonstrates durable and reproducible EUV emission without observable degradation of either the cathode or anode.ConclusionsThe CNT-based C-beam EUV source offers a compact form factor, low operating power, debris-free operation, and high temporal stability. These characteristics make it a promising candidate for actinic metrology and semiconductor inspection systems that require highly reproducible EUV emission and long operational lifetimes.</jats:p>
title: Development of a cold electron-beam-driven compact EUV source for next-generation inspection tools. Part I: design, fabrication, and evaluation of long-lifetime and reproducibility of source

items.abstract: <jats:p>As extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography advances at 13.5 nm with numerical apertures (NA) of 0.55 and higher, the effects of large incidence angles on multilayer design, wavelength selection, and NA limits are examined. Much of this is driven by EUV multilayer (ML) design, which should be optimized for large-angle applications to achieve maximum angular and spectral bandwidth. Reflectance amplitude and phase-shift analyses of Mo/Si multilayers are performed for angles corresponding to 0.55–0.75 NA EUV lithography, demonstrating the importance of accounting for phase effects. Understanding higher-order phase contributions reveals that defocus and spherical aberration originate from the mask multilayer itself, as confirmed through transfer matrix method (TMM) design and rigorous coupled-wave (RCWA) analysis. A depth-grading approach to large-angle multilayer optimization is introduced, leveraging the EUV optical properties of the constituent materials to improve performance by adjusting the material ratios within the stack. Results are presented for solutions using Mo/Si and Ru/Si multilayers for 13.5 nm high-NA and hyper-NA EUVL. Considering polarization effects starting at high NA—both at the mask object plane and the resist image plane—alternative large-angle Ru/Be multilayer configurations operating at 11.3 nm are also evaluated. The introduction of an 11.3 nm/0.63 NA lithography option mitigates some polarization-induced degradation observed at 13.5 nm/0.75 NA and offers an additional increase in focal depth. Design strategies for depth-graded multilayers for optical coating and mask applications are detailed.</jats:p>
title: Optical considerations of EUVL wavelength, NA, and multilayers at large angles

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundA key challenge in semiconductor 3D integration is the occurrence of small voids with diameters ranging from a few nanometers to several micrometers. Depending on the chip/package design and production process, these voids may occur across a large depth range (1 to 1000 μm)—e.g., the typical bond interface depth in wafer-to-wafer bonding lies at a depth of 775 μm. The standard tools to detect these deep defects are infrared microscopy, scanning acoustic microscopy (SAM), and X-ray. However, they all have limitations in resolution or penetration.AimHere, we propose an acoustical technique named half-wavelength contact acoustic microscopy (HaWaCAM®) to sidestep this problem. HaWaCAM® consists of a 4 GHz transducer integrated on top of a custom-designed probe and uses solid-to-solid contact to couple waves into the sample, enabling a higher detectability and resolution compared with SAM.ApproachIn this work, we investigate the suitability of HaWaCAM® to detect deeply buried voids. We used the HaWaCAM® setup on a silicon wafer sample containing programmed voids of different sizes buried below 49 μm of silicon.ResultsWe show that HaWaCAM® successfully detects voids down to a width of 0.75 μm at a depth of 49 μm. The signal-to-noise ratio varied from 30 to 45 dB, 20 to 30 dB, and 15 to 30 dB for void widths of 2.5, 1, and 0.75 μm, respectively.ConclusionsWe demonstrate the capability of HaWaCAM® to detect voids buried at large depths. We expect the current HaWaCAM® setup to detect voids with 2.5 μm widths with 6 dB SNR buried below >800 μm of silicon.</jats:p>
title: Suitability of half-wavelength contact acoustic microscopy to detect deeply buried voids

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundThe current carbon hard mask (CHM) film deposition techniques are not suited for mitigating x-field and x-wafer thickness and topography variation. This variability also affects both lithography patterning and post-etch critical dimension (CD) variability. Strategies to address this issue often include restrictive design rules, CHM polish, a more complex process flow. However, these solutions end up negatively impacting yield, cost, and process development cycle times. Canon’s work on nanoimprint lithography has led to the development of inkjet adaptive planarization (IAP). IAP provides planarization performance that is agnostic to feature size, aspect ratio, or pattern densityAimWe aim to collect data from wafers coated with IAP and other current available CHM-like techniques to characterize the impact of systematic local topography on the patterning process window.ApproachTopography data (AFM, Interferometry) as well as patterning data from wafers with IAP and CHM-like planarization is presented.ResultsAFM scans across 15% and 75% pattern density regions on the field demonstrated a 10× reduction in topography with IAP compared with other CHM-like planarization methods. Full-field interferometry data with ∼2.5 μm pixel size and noise levels of ∼5 nm show that IAP planarized wafers have x-field topography that is within ±5 nm. The patterning data that were collected were also consistent with an increase in the process window for the IAP planarized wafer.ConclusionsAs semiconductor manufacturing moves to more advanced nodes, CD variation plays an increasingly important role in determining whether performance and yield targets are achieved. Our data show that IAP can generate significantly flatter surfaces, which results in a wider process window, underlining the importance of controlling incoming wafer topography for critical layers.</jats:p>
title: Control of topography for scanner patterning using inkjet adaptive planarization

Measuring the destruction or removal efficiency (DRE) of point-of-use abatement systems is essential to account for gains realized by emissions reduction initiatives, but the traditional approach of hiring a third-party to perform these measurements is expensive and slow.AimThe focus of this project was the development of an in-house DRE measurement system that automates data collection, analysis, and reporting, aligned with the protocol Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) 430-R-10-003 but faster and more cost-effective than third-party measurement.ApproachThis development was achieved by identifying key requirements based on the EPA protocol, surveying available technologies, selecting an instrumentation supplier to collaborate with, and iterating on the design to achieve the specified requirements.ResultsA system was developed that enabled in-house real-time DRE measurement and reporting—significantly reducing cost, personnel hours, and equipment downtime required to perform these measurements on a large scale.ConclusionsThis system makes it feasible and cost-effective to measure the substantial number of abatement units required to determine actual abatement efficiencies and realize gains achieved from emissions reduction initiatives.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, the importance of high-sensitivity inspection using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) is increasing as the size of critical defects decreases, making efficient process control essential. Sensitivity and throughput are key metrics for defect inspection. SEM images with higher signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) generally yield higher sensitivity. However, acquiring high-SNR images typically requires imaging conditions that reduce throughput. If an inspection method can maintain high sensitivity even with low-SNR images, inspections can be performed under high-throughput imaging conditions. Therefore, improving robustness to noise is an important challenge. We propose an unsupervised deep-learning-based defect inspection method with strong noise robustness. The proposed method uses a multiple-reference estimation model to generate an arbitrary number of nondefective reference images from a single inspection image. The model reconstructs defective regions of the inspection image as nondefective while leaving nondefective regions unchanged. By averaging the multiple estimated reference images, the method produces a reference image with improved SNR. Defects are then detected based on the difference between this averaged reference image and the original inspection image. Evaluations on low-SNR SEM image datasets of line-and-space semiconductor patterns demonstrate that the proposed method improves robustness to noise for detecting small edge-deformation defects under the evaluated conditions.</jats:p>
title: Noise-robust SEM-based defect inspection via unsupervised learning to estimate multiple-reference images

items.abstract: <jats:p>BackgroundAs integrated circuit technology nodes advance, optical proximity effects distort printed patterns and degrade yield. Existing inverse lithography technology (ILT) struggles with multi-scale feature imbalance, sub-resolution assist feature (SRAF) incompatibility with main patterns, and the trade-off among optimization efficiency, printing accuracy, and mask manufacturability.AimThis work proposes an efficient gradient-driven ILT framework to address the above issues, improving printing accuracy, optimization efficiency, and mask manufacturability for advanced technology nodes.ApproachWe propose MF-ILT, a framework synergizing multi-scale adaptation and frequency-domain segmentation. It integrates two core modules: (1) a statistical multi-scale soft attention (SMSA) mechanism that adaptively fuses multi-scale features via feature variance metrics, avoiding manual weight tuning, and (2) a frequency-domain split SRAF (FS-SRAF) module that generates SRAF in high-frequency edge regions and suppresses isolated artifacts. The framework also adopts an improved hybrid loss function (Huber loss + process variation band regularization) and end-to-end differentiable design to ensure efficient gradient propagation.ResultsOn the ICCAD13 dataset and large-scale layouts, MF-ILT outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods: compared with gradient-driven methods, the average L2 error achieves a maximum reduction of 35.3%, and edge placement error (EPE) violations decrease by up to 48.6%; compared with deep-learning-based methods, the L2 error drops by 31.4% to 33.4%, and EPE violations decrease by 73.2% relative to the optimal deep-learning-based SOTA. The average optimization time per test case is only 3.1 s, with a peak memory consumption of 3.9 GB.ConclusionsMF-ILT provides an efficient and robust ILT solution for advanced technology nodes, with its core modules (SMSA and FS-SRAF) effectively solving multi-scale imbalance and SRAF incompatibility issues while balancing optimization efficiency and mask manufacturability. It lays a foundation for subsequent extensions to large-chip optimization.</jats:p>
title: MF-ILT: efficient gradient-driven inverse lithography technology with multi-scale adaptation and frequency-domain segmentation synergy

items.abstract: <jats:p>Complementary field-effect transistor (CFET) architectures stack n- and p-type devices vertically, creating buried features that challenge conventional metrology. A critical module is the selective SiGe lateral recess, which defines the inner-spacer width and strongly impacts device performance. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and optical scatterometry provide valuable insight but face limitations in throughput, scalability, or sensitivity for recessed structures. We demonstrate micro-spot X-ray fluorescence (μXRF) as a non-destructive wafer-scale method to quantify SiGe recess depth in device-relevant CFETs. items.abstract: <jats:p>Recently, ASML’s EXE:5000 scanner has become operational, which uses a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.55, which is 67% higher than the 0.33 NA of the current generation of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) scanners. This higher NA results in the printing of smaller features, which is essential for advancing semiconductor technology and sustaining Moore’s law. However, as NA increases, the incidence angles on the wafer also increase, leading to a stronger variation of the aerial image through focus, thereby reducing the depth of focus (DOF). Due to a limited focus control in the scanner and the finite resist thickness, this reduced DOF could result in a pattern failure. We explore the enhancement of DOF in high-NA EUV lithography, particularly within the framework of logic metal clips and their building blocks, i.e., dense and isolated lines, and tip-to-tip (T2T) features, using a dark field mask and a negative tone resist. We explain through simulations and experiments that the overlapping DOF of pitch 20, 40, and 60 nm horizontal lines and spaces can be significantly enhanced using three strategies: illumination source optimization, application of a hammer head to line ends, and application of a low-n mask absorber. In addition, we clarify how these three strategies significantly improve T2T printing performance in terms of CD control and local CD uniformity. In conclusion, we show that through a rational application of the three optimization strategies, an acceptable overlapping DOF can be achieved.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The processing environment has a significant effect on the performance of metal oxide resists (MORs). Here, we examine the effects of relative humidity (RH) and atmospheric oxygen on the morphology, chemical composition, and line/space (L/S) patterning results of indium(III) nitrate hydrate (In(NO3)3·xH2O) MORs. Previous work shows that processing In(NO3)3-based resists under ambient conditions at RH≥40% produces localized surface protrusions at the nanoscale, which disrupt L/S patterns by breaking the lines and increasing line-edge roughness (LER) and line-width roughness (LWR). We find that processing in a humidity-controlled glovebox at or below 35% RH eliminates the nanoscale protrusions. Independent variation of the spin-coating and post-application bake environments further shows that these defects form only when both processing steps are performed in humidities above 35% RH. Transmission Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy reveals no discernible compositional differences among films prepared in compressed air and nitrogen, whereas decreasing RH produces stronger spectral contributions from precursor components, including nitrate, ammonium, and water species. These results indicate that resist morphology and chemistry are more sensitive to moisture than to oxygen during processing. L/S patterns are subsequently fabricated using 100-eV electron beam lithography. Resists processed in the humidity-controlled glovebox at 25% and 35% RH exhibit defect-free lines with significantly lower LER/LWR values compared with those processed in the ambient laboratory environment at 40% RH. We have achieved a minimum LER of 3.7 nm±0.4 nm and an average line width of 18.9 nm±1.9 nm. We demonstrate that controlling the processing environment can suppress patterning defects caused by morphology and improve the performance of In(NO3)3-based resists, highlighting process control as an important consideration in the development of MORs for extreme-ultraviolet lithography.</jats:p>
title: Minimizing line/space pattern defects and roughness of indium nitrate resists through environmental control

items.abstract: <jats:p>The semiconductor manufacturing industry is characterized by high energy consumption and stringent operational requirements, making energy efficiency a critical concern for both cost reduction and environmental sustainability. We explore how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies can be leveraged to uncover hidden energy-saving opportunities and enhance the energy efficiency of facility systems in semiconductor plants. Through the integration of advanced data analytics, predictive modeling, and real-time optimization, AI/ML solutions can analyze complex operational datasets to identify inefficiencies, predict equipment performance, and suggest actionable improvements. Case studies and pilot implementations demonstrate how AI-driven insights enable smarter control of heat recovery as well as chiller and compressor systems, leading to significant reductions (6.5% and 10% validated annualized savings, respectively) in energy usage without compromising production quality or reliability. We also discuss challenges related to data quality, system integration, and model interpretability while highlighting the potential of AI/ML to drive sustainable innovation in semiconductor manufacturing facilities. The contribution of this work is an integrated, multi-level ML framework combined with expert validation, risk-governed deployment, and International Performance Measurement and Verification Protocol-aligned measurement and verification, enabling demonstrated energy savings across multiple fab utility systems.</jats:p>
title: AI-ML approach to uncover “hidden factory” of energy saving opportunity in semiconductor facility systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>High-index immersion fluids were extensively explored nearly two decades ago as a means of extending the resolution of 193-nm immersion lithography, but their further development was limited by challenges in optical, material, and fluid properties. Here, we revisit this concept with the aim of enhancing imaging performance within the constraints of existing scanner platforms. Although polyols and inorganic salts exhibit either increased absorption or insufficient transparency at the concentrations required for index enhancement, sulfonate-based systems provide a more favorable balance of optical and fluid properties. Among them, ammonium methanesulfonate (AMS) demonstrates the best overall performance, with a refractive index of 1.525 at 50% concentration while maintaining high transmittance at 193 nm, low viscosity, and favorable wetting behavior. AMS also shows no measurable increase in resist leaching and maintains stable optical performance under irradiation. Optical lithography simulations further show that AMS improves optical matching by reducing reflection, particularly for the dominant transverse electric component, and provides increased depth of focus while maintaining a comparable peak normalized image log slope relative to water. These advantages persist at numerical apertures up to 1.45, supporting the potential of AMS-based aqueous solutions as a practical route toward high-numerical-aperture 193-nm immersion imaging beyond the conventional water-immersion limit.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents the design, integration-oriented characterization, and validation of a capacitive sensing system for integration into additive-manufactured (AM) anatomical models used in medical training. A complementary metal oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) application specific integrated circuit (ASIC) sensor fabricated in 65-nm technology implements a wide-band Class-D driver and a differential current-measurement unit. The architecture supports electrical capacitance tomography (ECT) over a 10 kHz-4MHz excitation band, enabling real-time monitoring of dielectric variations caused by contact or proximity of surgical tools. Experimental results confirm the sensor’s sensitivity and demonstrate its viability when integrated into anatomical models.</jats:p>
title: Embedding capacitive proximity sensors into 3-D printed medical models for training applications

items.abstract: <jats:p>At present, there are only a limited number of scientifically sound methods for designing task-specific lighting systems, as well as techniques for measurement- and recognition-based image processing. A review of the literature shows that the systematic development of such systems has not yet been sufficiently investigated. Only a few published works describe methodological approaches that cover the entire process from the physical fundamentals through the requirements to the design and manufacture. Based on application-specific requirements, this paper presents a physically sound method for the systematic development of spectral lighting systems for measurement and recognition technology. The proposed new method combines existing principles and procedural elements from lighting technology, illumination optics and optical modelling into a structured workflow. The new method is applied and validated using the example of the development of a multispectral ring light for high-precision optical geometric measurements. The results show that the method provides a structured basis for the development and evaluation of spectral illumination systems for image-processing-based measurement and recognition applications.</jats:p>
title: A contribution to the design of spectral lighting systems for optical measurements and technical detection

items.abstract: <jats:p>A wide variety of data sources and AI-structured information and knowledge technologies serve as instruments for the exercise of government power. Lacking generally accepted categories for thinking about how we relate to and engage with such instruments of power, we cannot make them accountable to—or communicate effectively about—the kinds of structural controls that might guide their use. Recent examinations of the scale and value of data as an instrument of power address the need to measure and track it in standardized and centralized ways. Arguments concerning the "structural law of data" and ways of "measuring the data" in a parochially restricted legal context make no mention of highly relevant metrological challenges and opportunities. The focus is, instead, on data treated statistically without reference to contextualized relations with instruments traceably calibrated to unit standards characterized by explanatory theories demonstrating clearly repeatable and reproducible understandings of the phenomena involved. Most pointedly, centrally planned statistical analyses are taken for granted as the only available option for achieving the goals of increased data transparency and accountability. No consideration of metrologically viable measurements of intangible human and social assets is offered though these point toward hopeful possibilities for extending the SI unit system and productive ways of framing governments’ capacities for wielding information- and knowledge-based instruments of power. Familiar scientific, legal, market, and communications categories could plausibly make these instruments transparent and accountable in a manner congruent with the irreducible complexity of the structural law of measurement and its implications.</jats:p>
title: The structural law of measurement

items.abstract: <jats:p>Evaluating mechanical strain is essential in engineering, whether for probing mechanical components or for maintaining structures such as bridges and wind power plants. Image-based strain measurement enables spatially resolved strain evaluation and, because it is non-contact, has the potential to make strain determination on moving parts easier than with wired methods. Previously, we presented a non-contact strain measuring principle based on tilted grating arrays fabricated with two-photon polymerization that enables long-term absolute strain measurement. The concept is based on white light illumination and camera read-out. Here, we present a first lab demonstrator including the fabrication and molding of the tilted grating arrays, confirming the strain-dependent spectral response. A simulation is used to derive theoretical results of the strain response, and the experimental strain sensitivity of the prototype is derived. By comparison of the measurement and theory, we derive a strain sensitivity of 0.96% over a measurement strain range of 0% to 4.5%, and a theoretical strain sensitivity of 0.08%. Our approach offers an elegant non-contact strain measurement capable of long-term measurements, since the tilted grating array provides an indication of an object’s strain once applied.</jats:p>
title: A prototype of a non-contact strain measurement system using tilted grating arrays

items.abstract: <jats:p>Additive manufacturing of glass using laser deposition (Directed Energy Deposition, DED) represents a promising approach for producing complex, three-dimensional structures that are difficult to achieve using conventional subtractive methods. In this process, a glass rod is melted by continuous CO<sub>2</sub> laser radiation in the continuous-wave (cw) mode at temperatures of up to 2000°C and deposited layer by layer. While the production of individual layers is achieved with process stability, significant challenges arise during multi-layer fabrication, particularly in the form of deviations between target and actual geometry as well as insufficient surface quality due to cumulative height errors. To address these challenges, the measurement of component geometry is of central importance. Advances in optical 3D measurement technology, particularly in the field of thermal sensing, enable highly dynamic and precise measurement of even transparent structures. These form the basis for improving reproducibility and component quality in the additive manufacturing process of glass.</jats:p>
title: Shape characterization of additively manufactured glass structures

items.abstract: <jats:p><p> Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly penetrating all spheres of human activity, and like any new phenomenon, this expansion can be either beneficial or detrimental. In higher education, the desirable and undesirable uses of AI are particularly important: it can significantly streamline the teaching process by saving time on routine tasks, but it can also devalue teaching if AI is abused as a substitute for knowledge and a deep understanding of the topic. </p> <p> Nowadays, there is a lot of material and information available on the use of AI in programming education or, more generally, in SW-oriented taught subjects. items.abstract: <jats:p><p> The machine-assisted diagnosis of skin cancer is now considered state of the art. As a rule, proven high-resolution color (RGB) camera technology is used for optical imaging of the skin, and the data obtained is analyzed using traditional methods or modern image processing techniques based on neural networks. </p> <p> This article presents methods to optimize the multispectral design of multimodal camera systems for that purpose. Since multispectral optical features are expected to be of crucial importance here, the focus is on multispectral imaging of skin areas. To this end, a new multispectral snapshot camera with an innovative multi-aperture approach (MAC) is used, combined with other imaging techniques to capture color texture and 3D information. To identify an application-optimized design, universally applicable algorithmic methods are presented that enable automatic configuration based on available spectral information regarding the application class and the system design, as well as known technological limitations or constraints. Our paper illustrates a holistic approach to image processing, in which the focus is on ensuring the availability of the best possible raw data by optimizing multispectral imaging for a specific class of problems. The proposed methods are evaluated using simulations in realistic scenarios to validate the subsequent implementation steps. </p> <p> The considerations and findings presented are part of the first phase of the funded <i>multiSKIN</i> project, whose goal is to develop innovative multispectral camera technologies as part of a multimodal camera array for optical dermatoscopy. </p></jats:p>
title: Methods for the application-optimized design of multispectral image sensors, using the example of an innovative multimodal camera approach for optical dermatoscopy

items.abstract: <jats:p>Daylight electroluminescence (dEL) and photoluminescence (dPL) imaging enable outdoor inspection of photovoltaic (PV) module defects, but their performance is limited by the intense solar background. The current study investigates the influence of narrow optical bandpass filters on SWIR-based dEL and dPL imaging of silicon PV modules. Three narrow bandpass filter configurations near the silicon luminescence peak and the corresponding atmospheric water vapor absorption band, with different bandwidths ranging from 10 nm to 50 nm, were selected to systematically vary the balance between EL signal transmission and solar irradiance suppression. The filters were spectrally characterized and evaluated for solar background suppression, luminescence signal transmission, and defect visibility under outdoor illumination. Outdoor measurements up to ~590 W/m² showed that a narrow bandpass filter near the atmospheric water vapor absorption maximum effectively balances solar background suppression and luminescence signal transmission, enabling reliable defect visibility in both dEL and dPL without lock-in amplification. While dEL is most effective for resolving fine defect structures, dPL provides strong contrast for extended inactive cell areas, indicating that the combined use of both methods offers the most comprehensive defect assessment. These findings highlight the importance of optical filter selection for robust daylight luminescence imaging of PV modules.</jats:p>
title: Daylight defect detection in PV modules using narrow bandpass filters

items.abstract: <jats:p>In recent years, a shift from classic fixed arm robotic manipulators towards mobile platforms with manipulators has been observed due to the increase in flexibility of tasks. More recently, the focus has shifted towards humanoid robotics. Whereas the dynamics of the legs and self stabilization of such bi-petal robots have been solved, the behavior of the humanoid arms needs further improvement to move more naturally and human-like. To overcome the hurdle of lack of natural arm movement, as a human does subconsciously, to keep balance while moving different parts of the body, we propose an experimental setup to collect arm and hand movement data from humans using a set of Color (RGB) and Color and Depth (RGBD) cameras via MediaPipe, but without needing any markers. A robotic arm manipulator with a custom soft robotics hand then mimics the movement and shows direct output for validation. In this way, several daily human manipulation tasks can be mimicked, recorded and used for training to eventually enable full autonomy in the future. We conducted experiments to quantify the accuracy of the mimicked pose, focusing on the end-effector pose (position and orientation) while monitoring the joint configuration. In our experiments, an accuracy of ±2.5<i>cm</i> was observed in all three axes (x,y,z); the orientation accuracy lies within ±10&deg;. The demonstrator has been tested during several internal lab dry runs (for data collection) and public demos (showcasing robustness and longterm stability, e.g. during the Long night of research in Austria). Our work will serve as a basis for future multi-arm tracking and mimicking approaches.</jats:p>
title: Towards human-like manipulation of robotic arms using reinforcement learning and stereo vision

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large-scale material extrusion (LSME) is increasingly used for applications such as mold making, furniture construction, and prototyping. In these processes, however, deposition deviations may accumulate from layer to layer, causing material waste, additional energy and processing time, and in the worst case the failure of large printed parts. This work presents a proof of concept for layer-wise defect classification in large-scale MEX using jointly acquired 2D texture and metric 3D information. After each layer is printed, the process is interrupted and the print bed is moved to the acquisition position. An active stereo measurement system is used to acquire both 2D texture information and metrically calibrated 3D geometry after each printed layer. The proposed representation is evaluated on hollow cuboid components printed from PLA containing 20 wt.% wood particles. The dataset contains 97 measured layers and covers three deposition states: normal extrusion, over-extrusion, and under-extrusion. A ResNet-18-based classifier with fused 2D and metric-3D input is used for layer-wise classification, and leave-one-layer-out validation is applied. Compared with 2D-only and metric- 3D-only inputs, the fused representation achieves the best performance, with a 3-class accuracy of 92.78 % and a defect-detection recall of 0.961. The results show that metric-3D information substantially improves layerwise defect classification and that 2D texture and metric-3D information complement each other for monitoring extrusion-related deposition states.</jats:p>
title: Metric 3D layer-wise defect monitoring in large-scale material extrusion: a proof of concept

items.abstract: <jats:p>Maintaining mobility in old age and in the event of illness is crucial to quality of life. The SmartRoll project is developing smart rollators with technological enhancements and assistive functions to reduce the barriers to independent activity for patients in in-patient care facilities. A key aspect of this is gait analysis, which is used to quantify mobility limitations and track their progression. SmartRoll utilises a camera-based, markerless system on the rollator that combines the advantages of mobile and precise stationary measurement technology. Depth cameras (ZED X mini) and a neural network (YOLOv8spose) are used to detect feet and key points. The AI was trained on a specific dataset which, despite its small size, delivers promising results. Using the speed of the human-rollator system, gait parameters such as stride length (sum of left and right step) and walking speed are calculated. The software architecture is modular and processes raw data through AIsupported feature extraction right through to visualisation. A comparison of the SmartRoll system with the RehaGait reference system showed good agreement in stride length (8% deviation) and walking speed (3% deviation). This underscores the reliability of the approach.</jats:p>
title: Camera-based gait analysis system for a smart rollator

<jats:p>Rolling contact fatigue is one of the main mechanisms limiting the service life of rolling bearings. Fatigue-related material changes often develop below the raceway surface before visible damage such as spalling occurs. Conventional reference methods such as X-ray diffraction provide valuable information on residual stresses and microstructural changes, but they are destructive and therefore limited for industrial condition monitoring. In this study, eddy current testing is investigated as a nondestructive method for detecting operation-induced subsurface material changes in bearing steel. Sections from a single-row ball bearing were examined, including one operated sample and three new reference samples. The eddy current response was compared with destructive X-ray diffraction measurements of residual stress and Full Width at Half Maximum. The operated sample showed a clear eddy current signal separation from the new reference samples, with the strongest difference occurring in the subsurface region around 0.3 mm. This depth range also showed pronounced deviations in residual stress and FWHM. Based on the FWHM values, a relative Fatigue Damage Index of approximately 0.78 was determined. The corresponding eddy current delta of approximately 1.3 V was used as a first non-destructive calibration point. The results show that eddy current testing can detect fatigue-related subsurface material changes and provide a basis for future material-statebased remaining service life assessment.</jats:p>
title: Predicting bearing fatigue with eddy current (NDT): detecting stress due to operation, remaining service life

items.abstract: <jats:p>Practical experience with sensor systems is essential in engineering education, yet providing scalable laboratory environments for large student groups remains challenging. This work presents a multi-interface platform designed to teach sensor systems through progressive interaction with virtual and physical systems. The platform integrates sensors, microcontrollers, network communication, and interactive interfaces. Students connect sensors such as Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs), rotary encoders, and infrared sensors to microcontrollers. The measured signals are transmitted via wireless communication to external interfaces where they control system behavior. The platform supports three complementary interfaces. First, the Unity Interface allows intuitive visualization and rapid experimentation with sensor-driven interaction in a safe virtual scene. Second, the Web Interface enables distributed interaction with a shared digital factory scene accessible through standard web browsers. Finally, the Robot Operating System Version 2 (ROS) interface extends the same sensing concepts to robotic simulation and real robotic hardware, where sensor signals influence the motion and behavior of robotic arms. The proposed platform enables a progressive learning approach in which students move from virtual experimentation to real-world robotic interaction. It demonstrates how modern sensor education can combine simulation and physical robotics within one unified platform.</jats:p>
title: A multi-interface platform for teaching sensor systems using Unity, web, and ROS interfaces

items.abstract: <jats:p>Skin hydration status is an important indicator of skin barrier function and overall skin health. Because water exhibits strong absorption in the short-wave infrared (SWIR) spectral range, particularly near 1450 nm and 1550 nm, variations in skin water content can cause changes in the reflected light signals at these wavelengths. In this study, a SWIR multispectral reflectance imaging system covering six wavelengths (980, 1050, 1200, 1350, 1450, and 1550 nm) was developed, and images of the dorsal hand skin were captured under three different skin conditions: untreated, acetone-treated, and wet compress-treated skin. Skin reflectance values were extracted from on the hand region after dark frame subtraction, white reference normalization, and flat field correction. Based on these reflectance values, multiple spectral features were constructed to characterize differences among hydration states. In addition, a 980 nm polarization imaging experiment was conducted, in which the degree of linear polarization (DoLP) of the reflected light was calculated to characterize the depolarization behavior of skin, thereby further investigating the relationship between polarization response and skin hydration status. The results showed that reflectance at most wavelengths increased after acetone treatment, with more significant changes in features related to 1450 nm and 1550 nm. After wet compress treatment, reflectance values and the spectral features tended to return toward the values from skin in untreated state. In the polarization imaging experiment, DoLP increased after acetone treatment, and decreased to the level of values from the untreated skin after wet compress treatment, indicating that reduced skin water content may preserve polarization of incident light. Overall, the results show the potential of SWIR multispectral and polarization imaging for assessing skin hydration status.</jats:p>
title: Skin dehydration assessment using SWIR multispectral and polarization imaging

items.abstract: <jats:p><p> Making thermally and hygrothermally critical zones in timber construction visible, measurable, and traceable through digital visualization remains a major challenge in the building sector. The main objective of the project presented in this work is to develop a concept for AR/VR-supported representation and analysis of temperature and moisture behavior in timber-based building elements. This is particularly relevant for wall constructions made from different timber-based materials, where material transitions, geometric discontinuities, and connection details can significantly influence heat flow and moisture transport. </p> <p> The work is based on a combined research and demonstration approach. On the one hand, the project presented in this work aims to define a technically sound measurement strategy for identifying system-critical stress points. On the other hand, a suitable visualization concept is to be established that can convey the results in an intuitive and scientifically sound manner. The planned demonstrator is therefore intended not only to support the analysis, but also to serve as a communication tool for a wider audience. </p></jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents an interactive educational platform designed to teach the principles of electrical, environmental, and physiological measurements within modern engineering curricula. Developed using the STM32 microcontroller, the system exposes students to the complete measurement chain by combining real-time environmental tracking (CO<sub>2</sub>, temperature, humidity, pressure) and biomedical parameters with interactive human-in-the-loop applications. In contrast to existing single-purpose educational platforms, the novelty lies in the breadth of an integrated, metrologically transparent measurement chain that students bring to life themselves rather than in any individual sensor. A memory training game based on addressable RGB LED arrays and a reaction time test transition the curriculum from passive data observation to an active-learning framework. Metrological performance is verified through reference testing inside a climatic chamber and custom low-pressure environments, allowing students to diagnose and software-compensate for systematic sensor errors and to evaluate Type B measurement uncertainties directly from datasheet specifications. The proposed system is designed to improve student motivation, deepen understanding of real-time software synchronization, and provide immediate practical feedback on algorithmic correctness and human-machine interface performance.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>One of the main factors contributing to damage to forest roads is water. Water enters the forest road through rainfall or flows down from higher elevations along the road and its surroundings. If water is detected on the road, immediate conclusions can be drawn regarding maintenance measures that serve to preserve the forest road in the long term and ensure its usability for forestry operations. As part of an automated system solution for forest road monitoring, methods for detecting water are being investigated. An existing prototype system is equipped with various sensors for assessing the condition of forest roads. This paper documents the systematic investigation of whether water on the road surface can be detected using the existing sensor technology. To this end, methodologically representative scenarios are developed and identified. The study begins with a homogeneous outdoor surface and is subsequently transferred to the real-world context of a forest road. A criterion for identifying standing water and distinguishing it from moisture-saturated edge areas was developed based on the raw data from the investigations.</jats:p>
title: Methods for remote detection of water on forest roads

items.abstract: <jats:p><p> This project “AI4Optics” addresses the challenge of knowledge preservation and utilization in small and mediumsized enterprises (SMEs) within the optical measurement industry. SMEs face the risk of losing valuable domain knowledge as experienced employees retire and industry requirements evolve. The project therefore aims to develop a domain-specific chatbot that enables efficient and secure access to internal company knowledge.<br/> The system is based on a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture, combining semantic search with generative language models. User queries are matched with relevant content from a locally hosted knowledge base, and the retrieved information is used to generate context-aware responses. Company documents—such as ERP data, technical manuals, and engineering records—are processed in a structured pipeline: segmented into smaller text units, converted into semantic vectors using embedding models, and stored in a vector database for efficient retrieval. This enables the chatbot to identify relevant information even when queries differ linguistically from the original sources. A key aspect of the approach is the use of a fully local data infrastructure. </p> <p> The chatbot can be deployed on-premise, ensuring that sensitive company knowledge remains on internal servers and is not transmitted to external cloud services. In addition to internal documentation, this concept can be extended to external but controlled datasets, such as conference proceedings—for example, those from IMEKO. Instead of publishing such content openly on the internet, it can be stored on a secure local server and made accessible through a dedicated chatbot interface. This would allow engineers and researchers to query the complete body of conference knowledge efficiently while maintaining full control over data access. Similarly, this system can be fully customised for a specific company and utilise its own company-specific database. It is therefore a completely independent system and can be adapted for any type of business.<br/> This approach addresses a growing concern: currently, many conference proceedings are published freely online, making them accessible not only to the research community but also to external AI systems. As a result, proprietary knowledge, innovative ideas, and engineering solutions may be unintentionally used to train third-party models, potentially leading to a loss of competitive advantage. By contrast, a locally hosted chatbot ensures that knowledge remains protected within a defined environment—accessible to authorized users, but not distributed publicly or absorbed into external AI ecosystems. Initial evaluations show that such chatbot systems can effectively support engineering-related tasks, including material selection, design decisions, and troubleshooting. They provide features such as natural language interaction, transparent source referencing, multilingual capabilities, and real-time response generation. Overall, the project demonstrates the strong potential of domain-specific, locally deployed AI systems to preserve critical knowledge, enhance process efficiency, and protect intellectual property, while enabling controlled and efficient access to valuable technical information. </p></jats:p>
title: AI4Optics: private, locally hosted AI chatbot for optical metrology that leverages AI advantages while protecting company know-how

items.abstract: <jats:p>Machine-learning-based artificial intelligence (AI) tools are widely applied in industrial visual inspection, especially for flexible and data-driven quality assurance tasks. As a consequence, future engineers must not only be able to use AI-based inspection tools, but also critically evaluate them as measurement and inspection systems. This paper presents a laboratory practice integrated into the bachelor-level course <i>Quality Management and Quality Inspection</i> in the <i>Mechanical and Production Engineering</i> program at Hamburg University of Applied Sciences (HAW Hamburg). In the laboratory, students develop an image-based classifier to distinguish intact from broken chickpeas using smartphone images and a web-based GUI tool for creating custom machine learning (ML) classification models without specialized technical expertise. The concept emphasizes data acquisition, data splitting, training and testing, as well as the influence of data quality on model performance. The educational effectiveness of the laboratory was evaluated through a feedback survey. The results indicate that the laboratory was particularly successful in increasing awareness of the influence of data quality on AI performance and in improving students’ understanding of model evaluation procedures and metrics. The presented concept demonstrates how AI-based visual inspection can be integrated into quality engineering education using minimal infrastructure while promoting a critical understanding of AI-supported inspection systems.</jats:p>

The system captures a 4.0 × 2.0 × 0.5 m³ measurement volume in under 0.5 seconds, achieving lateral point spacing ≤ 2 mm and absolute 3D errors below 1 mm. The development of a robust and easy-to-use calibration procedure enables daily use by the sheet metal press operator, making the developed system ready for industrial deployment.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p><p> This paper presents the design, simulation, and experimental characterization of a distributed acoustic membrane sensor based on fiber segment interferometry (FSI). A custom fiber Bragg grating (FBG) chain was bonded onto a circular Mylar membrane, enabling simultaneous strain measurements at seven spatially separated sensing segments along a single optical fiber. A finite element model implemented in a multiphysics simulation environment was used to analyze membrane deformation, strain distribution, and vibroacoustic modal behavior before fabrication. </p> <p> The prototype was characterized regarding frequency response, pressure linearity, sensitivity, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), total harmonic distortion (THD), directional behavior, and spatially resolved vibroacoustic mode shape detection. At 300 Hz, the cumulative fiber signal achieved a sensitivity of 5.4nmPa<sup>−1</sup> with a linearity error below 1.25 %. At 1 kHz and 106 dB sound pressure level (SPL), an SNR of 55.2 dB, calculated using a spectral peak-to-noise-floor approach commonly reported in optical microphone studies, and a THD of 0.69% were measured. </p> <p> The segment-resolved FSI signals enabled identification of membrane modes up to approximately 1.5 kHz. In addition, the fiber position outside the neutral membrane plane allowed the membrane motion direction to be determined for sufficiently small deflections, while larger deflections led to a rectification effect consistent with Kirchhoff–Love plate theory. The results show that FSI-based membrane sensors can combine acoustic sensing with spatially resolved modal analysis using a single optical fiber. </p></jats:p>
title: Design and characterization of an acoustic sensor based on fiber segment interferometry

items.abstract: <jats:p>This work presents a correction model for a multispectral method for 2.5D shape measurement, based on the Shape from Focus principle. Using a monocular imaging system of a filter wheel camera, depth information is derived from the respective focus position. Both lateral (2D) and axial (<i>z</i>-axis) measurement accuracy must be ensured, which are limited by the occurrence of optical aberrations. These errors arise when capturing a stack of images with a multispectral camera using a moving image sensor, where the axial movement of the sensor leads to geometric distortions and other imaging errors. The method is performed with standard lenses (wide-angle lenses with endocentric design, constant numerical aperture, fixed focal length and aperture), with the aim of capturing a large field of view, which increases flexibility and practical applicability but introduces uncertainty regarding measurement accuracy. The aim is to demonstrate the efficiency of the presented correction model, based on affine transformations, with such standard lenses, to determine the optimal degree of approximation, and to identify the number of physical reference points required to correct 3D distortion at each <i>Z</i>-position of the image sensor, thus enabling precise 3D measurements. A key feature of this approach is that the image sensor is moved for both focusing and 3D scanning. The central challenge, therefore, lies in compensating for optical aberrations – the magnification varying across the working range, the object-distance-dependent distortion in 2D, and the focus-dependent <i>z</i>-distortion – to achieve reliable and accurate measurement results.</jats:p>
title: Mathematical correction model for image aberrations in 3D multispectral image data acquisition

items.abstract: <jats:p>Yellow emitting lasers are highly suitable for retinal disease treatment due to their high retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) absorption, enabling precise tissue heating without causing collateral thermal damage. Diabetic macular edema (DME), a leading complication of diabetic retinopathy affecting millions worldwide, is widely treated using laser photocoagulation to reduce vascular leakage. However, wavelengths such as 810 nm and 532 nm carry inherent risks of deep choroidal penetration or excessive absorption in non-target layers. To optimize clinical application and mitigate these risks, this study developed a comprehensive, two-dimensional axisymmetric computational human eye model using COMSOL Multiphysics. The model couples geometric optical ray tracing with the Pennes bioheat equation to simulate precise laser-tissue interactions. Our comparative thermal analysis of 532 nm, 577 nm, and 810 nm wavelengths confirms that the 577 nm yellow laser successfully localizes heat at the RPE while sparing the choroid. Furthermore, this model allows for the systematic optimization of critical micropulsed laser parameters, such as pulse duration, duty cycle, total time, and peak power. By identifying the parameter thresholds necessary to maintain target tissues within the 60-80°C therapeutic window while keeping surrounding neural retina below 45°C, this study provides a robust framework for maximizing both therapeutic efficacy and ocular safety in clinical settings.</jats:p>
title: Thermal and optical modeling of retinal diseases treatment utilizing yellow lasers

items.abstract: <jats:p>With the growing demand for accurate surface geometry characterization in advanced manufacturing and biomedical applications, reliable 3D imaging under complex illumination conditions has become increasingly important. Nevertheless, strong subsurface scattering and interreflections often corrupt the measured signals, limiting the accuracy of conventional optical sensing techniques. Here, we propose a windowed parallel single-pixel imaging (W-PSI) framework that reconstructs 3D geometry through light transport modeling rather than direct phase decoding. By analyzing the frequency response of global illumination, optimal spectral windows are selected to retain geometrysensitive information while suppressing redundant measurements. Experiments on highly scattering jade samples demonstrate robust and accurate 3D reconstruction. Compared with full-spectrum PSI, the proposed method significantly improves measurement efficiency while maintaining reconstruction accuracy, offering a general framework for 3D imaging in globally illuminated scenes.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Contactless vital-sign monitoring can improve comfort and hygiene in long-term, sleep, home, and clinical monitoring, but robust estimation of heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), and oxygen saturation (SpO<sub>2</sub>) remains a coupled sensing and algorithmic problem. This paper summarizes our research line on remote photoplethysmography and vital sign measurement using 3D-multispectral multimodal imaging. We first review the CoViTal system, which integrates RGB, NIR, thermal, and 3D imaging for registered multimodal acquisition and 3Dsupported ROI tracking. We then describe a miniaturized multispectral multi-aperture camera (MAC) as a compact extension toward portable and home-oriented monitoring. Based on these systems, we organize the preprocessing pipeline, HR estimation from multispectral rPPG, RR estimation from thermal and rPPG signals, SpO<sub>2</sub> estimation with spatiotemporal learning, multi-task learning, and domain-adaptive oximetry. Clinical validation with PSG reference showed second-level MAEs of 2.17 bpm for HR, 2.09 bpm for RR, and 1.38% for SpO<sub>2</sub> during oxygen desaturation events. MAC-based validation further demonstrated feasible RR, HR, and SpO<sub>2</sub> estimation with a trade-off setup. These results indicate that multispectral imaging can support both clinical monitoring and future home-oriented deployment, although challenges remain in motion robustness, clinical data coverage, cross-domain generalization, and real-time operation.</jats:p>
title: Photoplethysmography and vital sign measurement using 3D-multispectral multimodal imaging

items.abstract: <jats:p>Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) extends conventional RGB imaging by measuring light in tens to hundreds of narrow spectral bands, often extending into the short-wave infrared. The resulting wavelength-dependent responses provide information about material properties and chemical composition, enabling material recognition beyond RGB appearance alone. Machine-learning-based HSI systems are typically trained under a closed-set assumption and may confidently assign previously unseen materials to known classes. Similar to RGB imaging, reliable out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is therefore crucial for trustworthy hyperspectral recognition. In this work, we investigate whether post-hoc OOD detectors developed primarily for RGB image classification transfer to hyperspectral material recognition. Using a standardized hyperspectral line-scan setup, we acquire object-level data on polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), and polyethylene terephthalate (PET), as well as previously unseen materials. A fixed spectral-spatial R(2+1)D network is trained on reduced hyperspectral data obtained from three expert-selected spectral regions, as typically used for such a classification task. We evaluate four categories of post-hoc OOD detection methods: output-based, feature-based, model-enhancement, and intermediate-feature methods on sensor-matched near-OOD objects and complementary cross-domain and synthetic shifts. The investigated OOD detection methods exhibit markedly different transfer behavior. Feature-based and intermediate-feature methods generally outperform output-based and model-enhancement approaches. Moreover, method rankings differ across AUROC, FPR95, and FPR99, showing that global ranking metrics alone are insufficient for deployment-oriented method selection. The results presented highlight the importance of representation-aware OOD detection and evaluation at high ID-retention operating points for reliable hyperspectral material recognition.</jats:p>
title: Beyond RGB: out-of-distribution detection for hyperspectral material recognition
