items.abstract: <jats:p><p> The increasing demand for sustainable textile recycling requires robust automation solutions capable of handling deformable garments and detecting foreign objects in cluttered environments. This work presents a digital twin–driven robotic sorting system that integrates grasp prediction, multi-modal perception, and semantic reasoning for real-world textile classification. A dual-arm robotic cell equipped with RGB-D sensing, capacitive tactile feedback, and collision-aware motion planning autonomously separates garments from an unsorted basket, transfers them to an inspection zone, and classifies them using state-of-the-art Visual Language Models (VLMs). </p> <p> We benchmark nine VLMs from five model families on a dataset of 223 inspection scenarios comprising shirts, socks, trousers, underwear, foreign objects (including garments outside of the aforementioned classes), and empty scenes. The evaluation assesses per-class accuracy, hallucination behavior, and computational performance under practical hardware constraints. Results show that the Qwen model family achieves the highest overall accuracy (up to 87.9 %), with strong foreign object detection performance, while lighter models such as Gemma3 offer competitive speed–accuracy trade-offs for edge deployment. </p> <p> A digital twin combined with MoveIt enables collision-aware path planning and integrates segmented 3D point clouds of inspected garments into the virtual environment for improved manipulation reliability. The presented system demonstrates the feasibility of combining semantic VLM reasoning with conventional grasp detection and digital twin technology for scalable, autonomous textile sorting in realistic industrial settings. </p></jats:p>
title: Digital-Twin-driven textile classification and foreign object recognition in automated sorting systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Reusing construction and demolition waste (CDW) plays a crucial role in preserving natural resources. To obtain recycled aggregates of the highest quality, it is important to examine both the properties of the original building materials and the composition of the construction waste. As part of developing an automated system for identifying the materials contained in recycled aggregates, the proportion of each material fraction must be determined. This requires estimating the volume and applying an assumed bulk density to calculate the corresponding mass. The objective of this study is to estimate the volume of recycled aggregates. For this purpose, a series of randomly captured two-dimensional (2D) shadow images was recorded during a horizontal throw. Since no additional spatial coordinate information is available, various methodological approaches are being explored and evaluated. The volume estimation using an analytical approach is compared with machine learning approaches applying feature-based, image-based, and fusion models.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Deep learning (DL) is widely used for object classification in industrial applications such as inspection, quality assurance, and safety monitoring. Although convolutional neural networks (CNNs) achieve high accuracy, their use in practice is limited by two major challenges: small, imbalanced datasets and the high energy consumption of GPU-based systems. These issues are especially critical in industrial environments. This work proposes a framework for industrial object classification under limited training data and energy constraints. In this framework, small datasets are expanded using generative data augmentation for the training of deep learning models, and the trained models are quantized to 8-bit and then implemented on edge tensor processing units (TPU) with low power consumption. An experimental study shows that a cross-class accuracy of 0.842 in mineral construction and demolition waste (CDW) classification was achieved with generative data augmentation, with significant improvement compared to a CNN trained only with original data. This confirms the feasibility of edge TPUs and the effectiveness of generative data augmentation.</jats:p>
title: Generative data augmentation for industrial object classification on edge tensor processing units

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a visual interaction pipeline for mobile robots that combines face-based identity recognition with gesture-based command input. The system uses onboard camera data to distinguish authorized and unknown persons and enables accepted users to issue simple static hand-gesture commands. Since robot-mounted cameras often capture faces from a low viewpoint and with limited resolution, six pretrained face recognition networks are evaluated under robot-specific imaging conditions. The experiments compare model size, inference time, recognition accuracy, and zero-misclassification performance. AdaFace achieves the most reliable recognition results and is selected for the final system. The complete pipeline is demonstrated in two scenarios: authorized interaction and target person search. The results show that vision-based authorization and interaction are feasible using onboard sensing, although camera resolution, illumination, viewing angle, and gesture robustness remain important practical limitations.</jats:p>
title: Towards secure and intuitive outdoor human–robot interaction using vision-based face authentication

items.abstract: <jats:p>We present an event-based vibro-mechanical sensing approach for classifying objects enclosed inside an opaque capsule under externally applied vibration. Hidden objects are probed with a sequence of controlled excitation modes, and the resulting capsule micro-motions are recorded by an event camera at high temporal resolution and low data rate. From the event stream, we extract frequency-domain features and classify the resulting samples with a linear support vector machine. On an 8-class classification task, the proposed method achieves a mean accuracy of 82.2% in five-fold cross-validation. Compared with a conventional high-speed frame-based setup at similar temporal resolution, the event-based representation reduces the data volume by approximately two orders of magnitude. These results demonstrate the potential of event-based vision for low-bandwidth vibro-mechanical inspection.</jats:p>
title: Event-based vibro-mechanical sensing for hidden object classification at ultra-low data rates

items.abstract: <jats:p>Drug recognition and air bubble detection are essential to guarantee a safe therapy administration to patients safety during parenteral artificial nutrition. This study presents a multi-parameter optp-fluidic sensing platform capable of simultaneously identifying fluid drugs and detecting air bubbles by making use of a laser diode, a disposable cuvette, and a position sensitive detector. Fluid identification is achieved thanks to the different refractive index of the drugs producing measurable displacement beam shifts on the detector, while air bubbles generate distinct time-domain signatures as they interrupt the light beam. The proposed sensing platform offers an efficient integrable solution suitable for automatic fluid administration devices, enhancing both safety and process monitoring.</jats:p>
title: A smart optical sensor for safe administration of parenteral nutrition

items.abstract: <jats:p><p> The newly developed Si-InGaAs multispectral imager enables simultaneous scanning of the visible light (VIS) wavelength range from 400 nm to 700 nm as well as the adjacent near-infrared (NIR) range from 700 nm to 1000 nm and the shortwave infrared (SWIR) range from 1000 nm to 1700 nm. This means that the entire detection range from 400 nm to 1700 nm can be covered with a single device. In contrast to previous solutions, which divide the spectral detection range into two regions, the new camera performs multispectral acquisition across the entire detection range. The division into individual channels takes place in both the VIS range and the NIR/SWIR range. The VIS range is divided into the three channels red, green, and blue (RGB) in the usual manner. The NIR and SWIR ranges are preferably divided into a total of fifteen channels. This achieves a subdivision into spectrally effective channels for the entire detection range. This enables unrestricted analysis of both the visible spectrum and the particularly relevant near- and short-wave infrared spectrum. The fifteen spectral channels in the VIS/SWIR range are provided by a filter wheel, whose individual filters can be easily replaced through a service opening on the device. This allows the multispectral camera to be quickly adapted to different applications. </p> <p> The invention is used in technical areas such as rapid material analysis as well as in biology, food science, agriculture, forestry, and medicine. </p></jats:p>
title: Si-InGaAs based multispectral imager

By tracking the demodulated phase variations of the fiber probe through RRI (Range-Resolved Interferometry), the relative vertical displacement between the UAV and the measured object can be continuously monitored with micrometer-level noise. The proof-of-concept experiment demonstrates the feasibility of motion correction for UAV-based optical measurements using flexible fiber-contact probes, thereby improving measurement precision and stability.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Industrial X-ray Computed Tomography (xCT) is widely used for nondestructive inspection and dimensional metrology of complex components, where acquisition parameters such as the number of projections strongly influence achievable spatial resolution. However, statistically supported guidelines that relate these parameters to reliable resolution remain limited. In this study, the influence of reducing the number of projections on the reliability and stability of selected spatial resolution metrics in industrial xCT is investigated using a resolution phantom manufactured by Quality Assurance in Radiology and Medicine GmbH (QRM). For each number of projections, multiple reduced projection subsets are generated from one reference measurement by varying the angular offset. After reconstruction of each subset separately into the corresponding 3D voxel volumes, 2D slice images containing the phantom stripe patterns are extracted. Image quality is then evaluated from these stripe patterns using relative stripe response and approximate Modulation Transfer Function (MTF) indicator based metrics. The results show that increasing the number of projections improves the relative stripe response. The approximate bar pattern MTF indicator shows that the median response level changes only moderately with the number of projections, whereas the Q1–Q3 range decreases as the number of projections increases. Thus, projection number mainly affects the repeatability and stability of the estimated frequency response rather than shifting its central value.</jats:p>
title: Reliability of spatial resolution metrics as a function of acquisition parameters in industrial x-ray CT

items.abstract: <jats:p>This work reports on preliminary research activities toward the development of a compact, cost-effective optoelectronic sensor designed for the real-time monitoring of uremic toxins during hemodialysis treatments. The proposed architecture is based on UV absorption spectroscopy at a targeted wavelength of 285 nm, strategically optimized for seamless, future in-line integration downstream along the spent dialysate fluid line. To validate the sensing principle, static absorption measurements were systematically carried out on synthetic aqueous solutions of three major biomarkers found in dialysate streams: <i>p</i>-cresol, uric acid, and human serum albumin. The realized laboratory prototype exhibits robust, concentration-dependent, and quasi-linear response profiles across clinically relevant concentration ranges. These preliminary results successfully validate the analytical sensitivity of the hardware architecture, supporting the feasibility of non-invasive, absorption-based optical sensing as a solid preparatory step toward quantitative, real-time, and personalized dialysis clearance monitoring at the point of care.</jats:p>
title: Toward optical sensing of uremic toxins during blood dialysis: preliminary experimental validation

items.abstract: <jats:p><p> Hardwood value chains increasingly require measurement continuity from standing broadleaf trees in forests to sawn boards in industrial processing plants. In forests, optical remote sensing—terrestrial laser scanning (TLS), airborne and UAV LiDAR, photogrammetry (Structure-from-Motion, SfM), and multispectral/hyperspectral imaging—has evolved from stand-level mapping toward tree-resolved 3D characterization. This enables non-destructive estimation of stem and crown structure, diameter-related stem metrics, height, above-ground biomass (AGB) proxies and quantitative structure models (QSM), and species composition, while highlighting persistent challenges such as occlusion, scan protocol dependence, and transferability across forest types. Reviews and syntheses show that TLS is increasingly treated as a structural reference for ecology and for cross-scale integration with UAV and airborne products, while species discrimination remains strongly driven by spectral cues and phenology-aware acquisition. </p> <p> In mills, rapid quality presorting of sawn hardwood boards must operate under harsh conditions (dust, vibration) and high throughput, while producing auditable decisions aligned with grading and optimization rules. Contemporary industrial practice increasingly combines complementary sensors—machine vision, 3D laser profiling/scattering, X-ray transmission, microwave/RF moisture sensing, NIR/hyperspectral approaches, and acoustic stiffness proxies—supported by real-time optimization software and machine learning. Standards-based moisture reference methods anchor calibration and traceability, while multisensor scanning has demonstrated feasibility for automated hardwood grading at industrial line speeds. </p> <p> This paper provides a structured state-of-the-art review, contrasts hardwood and softwood sorting paradigms, discusses current hardwood construction products motivating higher and more reliable sorting, and outlines future research and engineering priorities for sensor fusion, uncertainty-aware calibration/validation, and closed-loop process integration from forest procurement to industrial optimization and the assumption that future, simpler, and more affordable technologies for the optical sorting of hardwood in microfactories will need to be developed. </p></jats:p>
title: Optical measurement of hardwood from forest to mill: remote sensing of broadleaf trees and industrial sensor-based presorting of sawn hardwood boards

items.abstract: <jats:p>The paper presents innovative teaching methods applied in teaching the course “Industrial Control Systems” to engineering students at the Technical University of Gabrovo, Bulgaria. This course is part of the curriculum of the Bachelor’s and Master’s degree courses in Mechatronics. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the course was taught traditionally with lectures and exercises accompanied by presentations. After 2020, the teaching team used MS Teams to deliver presentations during the distance learning sessions. The experience gained during this period opened new opportunities, and the professors developed a customized website for the course. This approach is very well received by the students because it offers access to educational materials anytime, anywhere, and using any electronic device. This increases the share of digital learning resources and improves the satisfaction of Generation Z and the upcoming Generation Alpha students who prefer this way of communication and learning. At the same time, the professors no longer have to send teaching materials by email and be concerned about file size, format, and other factors that limit their usability. The main benefits of this approach can be adapted by other professors in their teaching and extracurricular activities.</jats:p>
title: Innovative teaching of industrial control systems for engineers

items.abstract: <jats:p>Compact multi-channel spectral sensors based on thin-film interference filters offer a low-cost, integrable alternative to dispersive spectrometers, yet their performance is too often assessed by channel count alone, an indicator blind to inter-channel crosstalk, filter bandwidth, and the underdetermined nature of the spectral measurement. We present a metrological framework that formalises the channel-wise measurement model, identifies the dominant Type B instrumental uncertainty contributions (interference-filter centre-wavelength tolerance, responsivity line-shape deviation, PGA gain tolerance, and ADC quantisation and noise), and propagates them from the digital-count domain to irradiance through the device calibration curve. From the same datasheet parameters, the framework derives two figures of merit: the inter-channel crosstalk matrix C and the effective number of independent measurements <i>M</i><sub>eff</sub>, obtained as the participation ratio of the eigenvalues of C. The uncertainty budget is developed in detail for the AS7343, a device with broad and overlapping filters, under three calibration scenarios of increasing effort, while the figures of merit are computed for both the AS7341 and the AS7343. Predictions are cross-validated against the experimental spectral reconstruction errors reported in our previous calibration study on xenon illuminants. Although the AS7343 carries three more nominal channels than the AS7341, the two devices share an almost identical effective channel count (<i>M</i><sub>eff</sub> = 7.05 versus 7.07) and reconstruct the xenon test source comparably, demonstrating that channel count is a poor predictor of metrological quality and that the proposed metrics offer a predictive, datasheet-level basis for sensor characterisation and selection.</jats:p>
title: Beyond channel count: metrological performance metrics for compact multi-channel spectral sensors

items.abstract: <jats:p><p> Hydrochorous seed transport is essential for the biodiversity and regeneration of river floodplains. Monitoring this fluvial seed transport might therefore be a crucial proxy for evaluating floodplain restoration success and for the early detection of invasive neophytes. However, such process-based monitoring has so far been severely limited by time-consuming analysis of germinating seeds.  </p><p> This feasibility study, conducted within the Yes!IndSeed project, presents an AI-supported system for the automated detection and taxonomic classification of hydrochorous diaspores. Diaspores were digitized under standardized conditions using high-resolution macro-imaging (Hasselblad X2D 100C, 100 MP). The technical core is a YOLOv11 instance segmentation pipeline. To evaluate performance under realistic conditions, the dataset deliberately retained speciesspecific morphological variation and natural organic degradation. Validation yielded a mean Average Precision (mAP₅₀) of 93.1% and an overall F1-score of 0.87. While heavily occluded micro-diaspores remain challenging, the results demonstrate the fundamental feasibility of automated diaspore detection in complex fluvial matrices and provide a robust foundation for future high-throughput monitoring applications. </p></jats:p>
title: High-resolution macro-imaging and YOLOv11 instance segmentation for automated hydrochorous diaspore detection in fluvial matrices: a feasibility study

items.abstract: <jats:p>High-finesse optical cavity spectrometers are powerful tools for precision molecular spectroscopy and fundamental metrology. When combined with cryogenic environments, these systems gain additional advantages important for high-precision measurements, such as reduced Doppler broadening of spectral lines, narrower Boltzmann distribution, and suppresses spectral interference from residual contaminants. In this work we present the research conducted within the European metrology project COMOMET, involving collaboration between the Central Office of Measures and Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń. Due to its simple structure, molecular hydrogen (H2) provides an excellent platform for testing highly accurate theoretical predictions based on quantum electrodynamics (QED) and enables searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model. Precision spectroscopic measurements of its transitions can therefore contribute to the verification of ab-initio molecular calculations and the improvement of fundamental constants. In addition to the development of cryogenic spectroscopy techniques, ongoing work focuses on improving the accuracy and robustness of spectroscopic measurements relevant for future frequency standards and SI traceability.</jats:p>
title: Fundamental optical metrology with cold H2 molecules within the COMOMET project

items.abstract: <jats:p>We report an event-camera-based optical 4D (3D+time) sensor and compare it with a classical frame-based counterpart while measuring dynamic scenes. Frame-based active stereo 4D sensors project a series of patterns per single 3D scan into a scene for parallel temporal coding of object surface points. This is comparable to the parallel measurement of a global shutter camera in 3D. At the same time, each of the cameras measures the scene's responses. Phase retrieval, temporal correlation, or other methods identify pixels in both cameras which have likely seen the same object point. This approach forbids significant object motion during a single scan for spatio-temporal consistency. Consequently, high projection rates, high frame rates, and high illumination power are necessary for measuring fast motion. We developed an event-based stereo 4D sensor to break this limitation. Event cameras don’t measure complete frames, but instead, each pixel monitors its incoming brightness independently. When a positive or negative change crosses a threshold, an event is reported, i.e. a small data package with the pixel’s coordinates, a high-resolution timestamp, and photometric information, most commonly the polarity of the change. Coupled with a specialized projector, our event cameras sequentially measure sparse slices of the scene, which can be thought of as a rolling shutter. Temporally corresponding events are used to triangulate and reconstruct 3D points with timestamps from these events. We show that our event-based approach coupled with motion compensation can scan slower than a frame-based approach to recover the same moving object, reducing redundancy in measurements.</jats:p>
title: Unrolling the shutter in 4D: exploiting sub-scan dynamics with event cameras for efficient dynamic measurements

items.abstract: <jats:p>Heterogeneous material streams in industrial environments are a significant challenge for reliable optical measurement and classification. In particular, construction and demolition waste (CDW) exhibits complex compositions that limit the performance of conventional RGB-based sensing systems, while hyperspectral imaging (HSI) provides high discrimination capability at the cost of increased system complexity and limited scalability. This work presents a knowledge-distillation-based framework for transferring hyperspectral information to deployable RGB-based optical measurement systems. A multimodal teacher model, combining RGB and HSI data, is used to learn high-dimensional spectral–spatial representations of heterogeneous material classes. A compact RGB-only student model is then trained using a combination of ground-truth supervision and temperaturescaled teacher outputs, enabling the approximation of task-relevant hyperspectral decision boundaries without requiring spectral input during inference. The approach is evaluated on paired RGB–HSI data of representative construction-related materials under a stratified group-wise cross-validation protocol. The results show that the best distilled RGB student configurations clearly improve over a frozen RGB baseline and achieve classification performance close to that of the multimodal fusion model. At the same time, the comparison with a fully trainable RGB baseline indicates that sufficient student trainability is a decisive factor for successful distillation. These findings demonstrate that knowledge distillation can transfer task-relevant high-dimensional measurement information into low-dimensional sensing systems while maintaining high classification performance with RGB-only inference.</jats:p>
title: Knowledge distillation from hyperspectral imaging to RGB for AI-enhanced optical measurement systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Due to complex, unstructured, and dynamic environmental conditions, the automation of forestry work processes is limited. The kinematic architecture, and typical industrial and forestry applications of commercially available walking robots, has been reviewed, and a catalog of requirements for use in forestry has been derived. To date, there are no standardized evaluation and measurement methods for natural terrain. Therefore, the focus is on developing a reproducible, metrologically sound evaluation methodology for four-legged walking robots in a forestry environment. To this end, the forest environment was systematically divided into geometric, mechanical, vegetation-related, and optical influencing factors, and a modular test environment was designed for the controlled variation of individual parameters. Experimental validation was carried out using the Spot system in laboratory and field trials. First, the anthropometry, range of motion, and various gaits of Boston Dynamics Spot were experimentally characterized to quantify the relationships between individual parameters such as running height, speed, and stride length. Subsequently, the influence of static friction, additional load, weight distribution, vegetation interaction, and visual disturbances on stability and locomotion behavior was investigated. The results show a significant dependence of movement stability on the coefficient of friction and ground compliance, nonlinear effects when the center of gravity changes, and sensory misinterpretations on reflective surfaces. In addition, increased control activity was observed in the case of vegetation-related mechanical resistance. The methodology developed enables a structured and comparable performance evaluation of walking robots in natural environments and provides a basis for future benchmark standards in the field of forestry robotics.</jats:p>
title: Metrologically guided evaluation framework for walking robots in forestry environments

items.abstract: <jats:p>Continuous hematocrit (HCT) monitoring is essential in extracorporeal blood circulation (ECC) for managing hemodilution and oxygen transport. An optical layout designed to enhance sensitivity to erythrocyte-induced light scattering is presented for non-invasive HCT monitoring during extracorporeal blood circulation. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated an increased sensitivity to HCT variations compared to standard transmission mode. Experiments on human blood (HCT [27, 50] %) confirmed the simulated trends and showed minimal dependence on oxygen saturation (SO<sub>2</sub>) over the [67, 99] % range (mean SO<sub>2</sub> sensitivity: -1.25 mV/%). Calibration against a commercial reference system resulted in a second-order fit with R<sup>2</sup>=0.99 over a broad range, indicating suitability for accurate, continuous HCT monitoring.</jats:p>
title: A scattering-enhanced optical layout for blood hematocrit sensing: Monte Carlo modeling and experimental validation

items.abstract: <jats:p>In the last decades the relevance of forest monitoring has become increasingly relevant. Therefore, the diameter at breast height is one of the most relevant parameters of forest trees. A diameter tape measure is currently used to determine this parameter. In this study we want to digitise this and evaluate accuracy and applicability by using a photogrammetric approach. The goSCOUT3D is used as a representative for high-resolution 3D scanners. An everyday consumer product with a suitable camera is used for comparison. Specifically, the main camera of the iPhone 14 Pro Max was selected because it corresponds to the state of the art at the time of our research. In total 30 spruce trees were measured and five recordings with both sensors were made for every tree. As a reference for the extracted parameter, we used a tape measure. For each recording approximately 100 images were taken by walking around the trees (360 degree) at about one metre. After measuring the trees, a 3D point cloud was generated for every recording using photogrammetric evaluation software. A Python program was implemented using the convex hull algorithms. These algorithms make it possible to determine the diameter at breast height robust and efficient. Additionally, the program automatically determines the necessary height of 130 cm in the generated point cloud. In this way, the diameter at breast height was extracted for each recording. The final results for both sensors were then evaluated and compared with the reference value of the tape measure. Compared to the iPhone 14 Pro Max, the goSCOUT3D delivers quantitatively better results for the diameter at breast height.</jats:p>
title: Evaluation of an approach to determine the diameter at breast height of forest trees using the goSCOUT3D handheld scanner in comparison to an iPhone

items.abstract: <jats:p>Dielectric elastomer actuators (DEAs) exhibit outstanding features such as excellent flexibility, large deformation, and high energy density, showing great potential in soft robotic applications. This paper focuses on a rolled dielectric elastomer actuator, emphasizing the structural design and fabrication process of the multi-layer rolled DEA. Systematic characterizations are conducted to investigate its key performances, including output displacement, blocked force and dynamic frequency response. To validate the practical actuation capability, the actuator is integrated with a pair of simple foot structures to develop a prototype of small-scale soft crawling robot. The directional crawling locomotion of the robot is realized by the periodic extension and contraction of the rolled DEA. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed rolled DEA possesses favorable soft actuation performance and structural stability, which can effectively drive the small robot to achieve continuous movement. This work verifies the application potential of the rolled DEA configuration in soft actuation and miniature robotic systems, and provides an experimental basis for the design and engineering application of soft actuators.</jats:p>
